The Unassailable Imperative: Why a 100% Land Value Tax Must Be Our Sole Revenue Source

Imagine a society where your labor is no longer taxed. Where the fruits of your ingenuity, your sweat, and your investment are yours to keep entirely. Imagine cities free from blight, where vacant lots vanish as owners are compelled to develop valuable land or cede it to those who will. Envision an end to the brutal cycles of boom and bust fueled by land speculation, and a world where crippling wealth inequality begins to heal not through punitive measures on productivity, but by rectifying a fundamental, ancient injustice: the privatization of community-created value. This is not a utopian fantasy; it is the tangible, scientifically sound, and profoundly just outcome achievable only by implementing a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land, as championed by Henry George and Georgist economics. This is not merely a tax reform; it is the ethical and economic foundation for a truly free, prosperous, and equitable society, and it must become the sole source of public revenue.

The core moral argument is unassailable: land value is not created by landowners; it is created by the community. The value of a plot of land in downtown Manhattan, a fertile valley, or even a remote wilderness parcel with future development potential stems entirely from factors outside the individual owner's control and effort. It arises from the collective presence of neighbors, the infrastructure built with public funds (roads, sewers, schools, parks), the security provided by police and courts, the vibrancy of the local economy, and the very existence of the community itself. When a landowner collects "rent" – the income derived purely from exclusive possession of a location – they are appropriating wealth generated by society as a whole. This is not a return on investment or labor; it is an unearned windfall, a massive, ongoing subsidy extracted from every resident who creates the value through their presence and productivity. To allow this rent to be privately pocketed is institutionalized theft from the community, the foundational injustice upon which much poverty and inequality are built. Taxing away 100% of this unimproved land value is simply the act of reclaiming for the community the value it alone created. It is a matter of basic justice, a restitution for centuries of communal wealth being siphoned off by passive titleholders. Keeping even a fraction of this rent for private gain perpetuates an immoral system where mere ownership, divorced from contribution, generates vast wealth.

Beyond morality, the economic efficiency of a pure 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) is unparalleled and transformative. Unlike taxes on wages, profits, sales, or buildings – which distort behavior, penalize productivity, and create "deadweight loss" – an LVT targets a factor of production that is fixed in supply and cannot be hidden or moved. You cannot produce more land. You cannot avoid owning land by working less or investing elsewhere. Therefore, taxing land value does not discourage its creation (because it can't be created) or alter beneficial economic behavior. It creates zero deadweight loss. The consequences are revolutionary:

  1. Eradication of Speculation & Blight: Holding land idle for speculative gain becomes financially impossible. Owners must either develop the land to its highest and best use (generating taxable income from improvements they do own) or sell it to someone who will. Vacant lots in prime locations vanish, replaced by housing, shops, and workplaces. Urban decay reverses as underutilized sites are activated. The boom-bust cycle fueled by land price speculation – the root cause of most major recessions – is broken at its source.
  2. Massive Boost to Productivity & Innovation: Removing all taxes on labor and capital (wages, profits, buildings, sales) unleashes unprecedented economic energy. Workers keep 100% of their earnings, incentivizing effort and skill development. Entrepreneurs invest freely, knowing returns on productive capital won't be taxed. Building and improving property becomes highly attractive, as the value of those improvements remains entirely with the owner. This flood of productive investment drives genuine economic growth, not asset inflation.
  3. Optimal Land Use: The market, guided by the LVT, automatically allocates the most valuable locations to their most valuable uses. A prime downtown site becomes a skyscraper, not a parking lot. Agriculture flourishes on the most fertile soil, as farming on marginal land becomes relatively cheaper (its unimproved value is low). This maximizes the total productive output of the economy and the well-being derived from scarce land.
  4. Simplicity & Reduced Compliance Costs: A single tax on a simple, measurable base (unimproved land value) eliminates the vast, costly apparatus of income tax collection, sales tax administration, and corporate tax loopholes. Valuation, while requiring effort, is far more stable and objective than assessing the value of complex, mobile capital or fluctuating incomes. The savings in bureaucratic overhead and compliance costs for citizens and businesses are enormous.

Critics raise predictable but easily dismantled objections. "What about farmers?" they ask. The unimproved value of truly rural agricultural land is typically very low; the LVT burden would be minimal compared to current property taxes (which often tax improvements like barns) or income taxes. The tax would primarily impact large landholders holding valuable development sites or resource-rich land idly. "Won't it crash land prices?" Yes – the speculative premium would vanish, revealing the true, site-specific unimproved value. Land would become far more affordable to use, as purchase prices would reflect only the value of the location itself, not decades of anticipated rent extraction. This is a feature, not a bug. "What about seniors on fixed incomes?" A well-designed transition could include deferrals or credits, recognizing that the tax replaces other burdens. Crucially, their incomes (from labor or savings) would no longer be taxed, providing significant offset. The core objection – that landowners have a "right" to the unearned rent – collapses under the Georgist moral argument: that rent belongs rightfully to the community that created it.

The case for making this the sole source of government revenue is compelling. First, the aggregate unimproved land rent within any developed nation is vast – studies consistently show it comfortably exceeds necessary public revenue, especially when freed from the distorting effects of other taxes. Second, relying only on LVT eliminates the perverse incentives and economic damage caused by all other taxes. As long as a single tax on labor or capital remains, it discourages that activity, distorts the market, and creates opportunities for evasion. Only a pure LVT system achieves the theoretical ideal of a perfectly efficient tax. Third, it creates a powerful feedback loop: because public spending (on schools, transit, parks) directly increases the land value captured by the tax, communities have a direct, transparent incentive to invest wisely in public goods that actually enhance locational value, rather than engaging in pork-barrel spending. Government becomes accountable for creating genuine value.

Implementing a 100% LVT is not a technocratic tweak; it is a civilizational correction. It rectifies the fundamental error of allowing private individuals to monopolize the value created by the community, an error that fuels inequality, stifles opportunity, encourages wasteful land use, and poisons our economy with speculation. It replaces punishment for productivity with a rational capture of the unearned increment derived solely from existence within society. The efficiency gains would unlock unprecedented prosperity; the moral clarity would restore faith in a just system. We have spent centuries taxing the lifeblood of our economy – labor and capital – while allowing the free-flowing spring of land rent, generated by all of us, to be diverted into private reservoirs. It is time to recognize land as the common inheritance it truly is. Implementing a 100% Land Value Tax as the sole source of public revenue is not merely economically optimal; it is the only fair, efficient, and ultimately sustainable foundation for a free and flourishing society. The imperative is clear, the principles are unassailable, and the time for action is now. Let us build the future on the solid ground of justice, not the shifting sands of unearned privilege.

Georgist Philosophy: The Case for a 100% Tax on Unimproved Land Value

(Based on Henry George's 1879 work, Progress and Poverty)

Georgeism (or Georgism) argues that a single tax on the unimproved value of land—levied at 100% of that value—should replace all other taxes (income, sales, property, etc.). Below is a factual breakdown of its core reasoning and supposed benefits, grounded in Georgist economic theory. Note: This is a theoretical framework; no jurisdiction has implemented it in full, though partial versions exist (e.g., land-value taxation in Pennsylvania, Estonia, and Taiwan).

Key Definitions

  • Unimproved land value: The market value of bare land (location only), excluding buildings, crops, or human-made improvements.
    Example: A vacant lot in downtown Manhattan vs. one in rural Kansas. The value difference stems from location (proximity to jobs, infrastructure, neighbors), not the owner’s effort.
  • Economic rent: Revenue derived from controlling a scarce resource (like land) without labor or investment. Georgists view this as "unearned income."
  • Not a tax on buildings/capital: Georgists oppose taxing improvements (e.g., homes, factories), arguing this stifles development.

Why Tax Only Unimproved Land Value?

Georgists claim this addresses a fundamental flaw in conventional taxation:

1. Land Value Is Created by Society, Not Individuals

  • Reasoning: Land value rises due to community activity (e.g., new schools, roads, population growth), not the landowner’s effort. Taxing this "unearned increment" recaptures wealth generated collectively.
  • Example: A city builds a subway station. Nearby land values surge—not because the owner improved the land, but because of public investment. Georgists argue this windfall belongs to the community.

2. Land Is Fixed in Supply

  • Reasoning: Unlike labor or capital, land cannot be "taxed out of existence." A 100% tax on land value (not quantity) doesn’t reduce land availability.
  • Contrast: High income/capital taxes may discourage work/investment. A land-value tax (LVT) only affects idle landowners, not productive activity.

3. Eliminates "Economic Rent" Extraction

  • Reasoning: Landowners profit from scarcity they didn’t create (e.g., holding vacant lots for speculation). Taxing 100% of unimproved value removes this incentive, directing wealth toward public use.

Supposed Benefits of a 100% LVT as Sole Revenue

✅ Eliminates Deadweight Loss

  • How: Most taxes (e.g., income, sales) distort behavior—discouraging work, saving, or investment. An LVT only taxes a fixed resource, so it:
    • Doesn’t penalize productivity (e.g., building housing or starting businesses).
    • Forces landowners to use land efficiently or sell it.
  • Result: Higher land utilization (e.g., fewer vacant lots), increased housing supply, and no market distortions.

✅ Ends Speculation & Land Monopoly

  • How: Holding land idle becomes costly (since tax = full unimproved value). Owners must develop land or sell to those who will.
  • Result: Reduced urban sprawl, lower housing prices, and less "land banking" (strategic hoarding).

✅ Fairer & More Efficient Revenue

  • Equity: Taxes fall on those benefiting from community-created value (e.g., prime-location owners), not workers or entrepreneurs.
  • Efficiency: Valuation is simpler than income/capital (land can’t be hidden or moved). Collection costs are low.
  • Revenue Stability: Land values rise with economic growth, ensuring reliable public funding.

✅ Stimulates Productive Investment

  • How: Without taxes on buildings/income, owners invest freely in development.
    Example: A developer won’t underbuild to avoid property taxes—since only land is taxed, they maximize structures to offset the LVT.
  • Result: More housing, commercial spaces, and infrastructure.

✅ Reduces Inequality

  • How: Captures wealth from inherited/location-based advantages (which drive inequality). Revenue funds public goods (e.g., UBI, services), lifting the poorest.
  • George’s view: Land is humanity’s common inheritance; privatizing its value is theft from the community.

✅ No Tax Evasion or Shifting

  • How: Land can’t flee offshore. The tax burden cannot be passed to tenants (rent reflects market rates, not taxes).
    Evidence: Studies (e.g., in Pennsylvania) show LVT lowers commercial rents by spurring development.

Why 100%? Why Only This Tax?

  • 100% rate: To fully capture all economic rent from land. Georgists argue even a 90% tax leaves unearned profit, perpetuating speculation.
  • Sole revenue source: All public funding (military, schools, etc.) should derive from this "social dividend." Other taxes penalize productivity and are redundant once land rent is fully socialized.

Criticisms & Real-World Context

  • Valuation challenges: Accurately separating "unimproved" land value from improvements is complex (though modern GIS/data helps).
  • Transition issues: Could displace land-poor rural owners (e.g., family farms) if not phased in fairly.
  • Political feasibility: Landowners hold significant power; historical attempts (e.g., 1930s U.S.) faced strong opposition.
  • Revenue adequacy: Critics question if LVT alone could fund large modern states (Georgists counter that land rent equals ~30-40% of GDP in developed nations).

Conclusion

Georgism asserts that a 100% tax on unimproved land value would:
① Rectify injustice by returning community-created wealth to the public,
② Boost efficiency by ending subsidies for land hoarding, and
③ Replace regressive/punitive taxes with a fair, growth-friendly system.
While untested at scale, its logic rests on the unique economic properties of land—as a fixed, socially created asset. As Henry George wrote:
> "The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe the air—it is a right proclaimed by the fact of their existence."

For deeper study: Read Progress and Poverty (1879) or explore modern analyses by the Henry George Foundation.

BREAKING: Local Man Furious His "Right to Hoard Barren Dirt" Overridden by Sensible Policy

By I.M. Ridiculous, Senior Satirist for The Land Value Times (Printed on 100% Recycled Taxpayer Sweat)

SPRINGFIELD, USA — Outraged citizen Barry McLandgrabb, 58, stormed his local town hall yesterday, waving a crumpled title deed like a white flag of economic illiteracy, demanding immediate exemption from the newly proposed 100% Land Value Tax (LVT). His crime? Owning five vacant lots downtown while actively lobbying against any development, ensuring his "investment" rots like forgotten turnips.

"THIS IS TYRANNY!" McLandgrabb bellowed, his face redder than a sunset over someone else’s productive farmland. "My property rights! I bought that dirt fair and square with money I made not building hospitals or schools! Now you wanna tax the value of the dirt itself? Preposterous! That’s like taxing my shadow for existing where the sun shines!"

Ah, yes. The sacred "Property Rights" argument. As if the divine right to hoard unimproved land—gained solely because Great-Great-Grandpa McLandgrabb squatted before zoning laws—trumps the community’s right to fund roads on that land. McLandgrabb’s logic is air-tight: "I own this plot because I saw it first, and since I’m doing nothing with it, it’s clearly my right to pay less tax than the guy running a bakery on an identical plot next door. Duh. Economics 101, pal."

The "Practicality" Panic: Because Measuring Dirt is Harder Than Herding Cats
Nearby, Dr. Penelope Piffle, an economist who’s never seen a spreadsheet she didn’t immediately misinterpret, wrung her pearls. "The impracticality!" she screeched into a megaphone shaped like a top hat. "How could we possibly separate the land value from the improvements? It’s like trying to weigh a cloud while riding a unicycle! Do you have ANY idea how complex dirt is? What if the land value is... sad?!"

Dr. Piffle, of course, has no issue with the current system where we tax buildings down to the last brick with terrifying precision ("Ah yes, this bay window adds exactly $12,347.50 to your tax bill!"), yet somehow believes land—a static, unmoving, non-produced asset—defies valuation. Her solution? Keep taxing labor and capital improvements into oblivion while letting land hoarders pay pennies for assets they didn’t create. Brilliant! It’s almost as if she’s being paid by the Barons of Barren Lot LLC… (Checks notes) Oh. She is.

The "Grandma’s Shack" Gambit: A Masterclass in Missing the Point
Meanwhile, Mayor "Slippery" Sal Scammons, whose campaign coffers overflow with "landowner donations," delivered a tear-jerking plea on the steps of City Hall: "Think of the widows! The veterans! Grandma Mabel, living in her 100-year-old shack on a hilltop—she’ll be homeless if we tax the land under her feet at its actual market value! This is class war!"

Ah, the beloved "Grandma’s Shack" gambit—the anti-LVT equivalent of yelling "Think of the children!" while quietly pocketing lobbyist cash. Never mind that:

  1. LVT systems EXEMPT or GRANDFATHER primary residences (Grandma keeps her shack, pays near $0 tax, and the city still gets funds from the speculator buying the hilltop beside her for a skyscraper).
  2. *Under current systems, Grandma *already pays high property taxes on her depreciating shack, pushing her out of her home today while the guy with 20 vacant warehouses pays pennies.
  3. If Grandma’s shack is on valuable land, she’s likely sitting on a goldmine she could monetize (e.g., sell to developers, move to affordable housing)—if the system didn’t incentivize hoarding. But hey, why let facts ruin a good sob story?

The "But Who Will Speculate?!" Emergency
The most hysterical cries came from the Speculators’ Union Local 666. "If you tax the unimproved value of land," wailed Chad Leverage, CEO of "We Buy Dirt (Then Do Nothing) Inc.," "then... then... who will speculate?! Who will buy land, sit on it for 30 years, jack up prices for everyone, and provide zero value to society?! This destroys innovation!"

Yes, Chad. LVT does destroy the "innovation" of doing nothing while the city builds roads, schools, and hospitals that make your dirt valuable. It’s a feature, you magnificent leech. Under LVT, you’d either:
A) Develop the land (providing housing/jobs),
B) Sell it to someone who will, or
C) Pay the full cost of monopolizing a community-created asset.
Imagine that—using land productively! How socialist!

The Grand Finale: "But... But... It’s Fair!"
The most damning evidence of anti-LVT delusion came when Henry George’s ghost materialized (as ghosts of dead economists do) and simply said: "Taxing land value costs the community nothing. It can’t flee, hide, or shrink. It’s the only tax that actually raises wages and lowers rents."

The crowd erupted in panic. "FAIR?!" McLandgrabb shrieked. "You can’t have a tax that punishes doing nothing! That’s... that’s merit! Where’s the merit in paying less tax than the guy who built a grocery store?!" Dr. Piffle faintly into a fainting couch shaped like a tax loophole. Mayor Scammons immediately proposed a new law banning dead economists from town halls.

Conclusion: The Emperor’s New Dirt
Let’s be clear: Opposing 100% LVT isn’t about "practicality" or "grandmas." It’s about protecting a rigged system where the biggest contributors to poverty, inequality, and urban decay—land hoarders and speculators—pay the least. They dress their greed in "property rights" and "complexity," but it’s just the emperor’s new dirt: invisible, absurd, and funded by your property taxes.

So next time you hear someone whimper about LVT, just smile and say: "Don’t worry, champ! Keep hoarding that vacant lot. We’ll just let the rest of us pay to build the roads, schools, and hospitals that make it valuable... while you call us the communists for wanting you to chip in. Sounds fair!"

The Unshackling of the Earth: A Call for Justice Through the Single Tax

It’s about recognizing that the earth, our common birthright, belongs to all of humanity – the living, the yet-to-be-born, and the community that sustains us all. Private land rent is the taproot of inequality. It siphons the wealth generated by society into the pockets of the few who held a lucky deed.

(Conclude with soaring, unifying vision)

We stand at a crossroads. We can continue down the path of escalating poverty, environmental degradation from sprawl, and the soul-crushing weight of taxes on the productive – all while the bounty of location, the gift of community, flows silently into private vaults. Or we can choose justice.

We can choose the Single Tax. Not as a mere policy tweak, but as a moral imperative. As the fulfillment of the promise that this earth, and the opportunities it holds, belong to all its inhabitants. Fund government from the value we create together. Liberate labor and capital. End the scourge of land monopoly.

Let us reclaim the earth from the rentiers! Let us build a society where every person shares in the common bounty they help create! Let us demand the 100% tax on land value – the only tax that is just, efficient, and capable of unleashing the true, abundant potential of humanity upon this shared, beautiful planet!

The time for half-measures is over. The time for the Single Tax is NOW! Let’s unshackle the earth and build a future worthy of us all!

The Case for a 100% Land Value Tax: Justice, Efficiency, and Prosperity

Introduction

Imagine a tax system that cannot be evaded, creates no economic inefficiency, reduces inequality, encourages productive development, and funds government entirely from a source that no individual created. This isn't utopian fantasy—it's the century-old proposal of economist Henry George: a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land. This essay argues that fully capturing land rent for public benefit represents not merely good policy, but a moral and economic imperative that would transform society by eliminating unjust privilege, maximizing economic efficiency, and creating broadly shared prosperity.

The Moral Foundation: Land as Common Heritage

The ethical case for land value taxation rests on a fundamental distinction: land is not the product of human labor. While individuals justly own what they create through their efforts, land exists independent of human action. As Henry George argued, "The equal right of all men to the use of land is as clear as their equal right to breathe air."

When private individuals capture the rental value of land—the premium society pays for exclusive access to location—they appropriate wealth created not by their own efforts but by the community. A vacant lot in Manhattan commands enormous value not because its owner improved it, but because millions of people built a city around it. The owner contributes nothing yet extracts tribute from those who would use that location productively.

This violates basic principles of justice. We don't grant monopolies on air or sunshine; why should location, equally a gift of nature, be different? Every person has an equal moral claim to the earth's resources. A 100% land value tax (LVT) doesn't confiscate legitimately earned wealth—it prevents the confiscation of communal wealth by private interests.

Consider two neighbors: one works tirelessly to improve her property, building structures and cultivating gardens; the other leaves his land vacant, waiting for surrounding development to increase its value. Under current systems, both may see property values rise, but only one created value through labor. An LVT ensures that self-created improvements remain with the improver, while the community-created land value returns to the community. This is not confiscation—it's justice.

Economic Efficiency: The Perfect Tax

From an economic standpoint, land value taxation is uniquely efficient because land supply is perfectly inelastic—there is only so much of it, and taxing it cannot reduce the quantity available. This distinguishes land from all other factors of production.

Eliminating Deadweight Loss

Every conventional tax creates deadweight loss by distorting economic decisions. Income taxes discourage work. Sales taxes discourage consumption. Capital gains taxes discourage investment. Corporate taxes discourage production. Each pushes economic activity below optimal levels, making society poorer.

Land value taxation creates no such distortion. Whether taxed at 0% or 100%, the same amount of land exists in the same locations. Landowners cannot hide land in offshore accounts, move it to tax havens, or reduce its supply. The tax captures pure economic rent—payment for something in excess of what's necessary to bring it into production—making it economically costless.

Nobel Prize-winning economist William Vickrey called land value taxation "the least bad tax"—but this understates the case. It's not merely less harmful; a 100% LVT actively improves economic efficiency by eliminating the incentive to speculate on and hoard undeveloped land.

Ending Harmful Speculation

Under current systems, speculators profit by withholding land from productive use, waiting for values to rise. This creates urban sprawl, as development leapfrogs over vacant or underutilized parcels held for speculation. Cities expand inefficiently outward while valuable central locations sit idle.

A 100% LVT makes speculation unprofitable. If land's full rental value goes to public revenue, holding land produces no private return unless it's put to productive use. Vacant lots in thriving neighborhoods become financial liabilities rather than speculative assets, forcing owners to develop, sell to those who will develop, or face mounting tax obligations.

This transforms land use patterns. Development concentrates where infrastructure already exists, reducing sprawl, shortening commutes, and lowering public service delivery costs. Housing supply increases as underutilized parcels are developed. Land prices fall (since the capitalized rental stream now goes to public revenue rather than private pockets), making home ownership more accessible.

Encouraging Productive Development

Current property tax systems penalize improvement. Build a house or factory, and your taxes increase. This perversely discourages exactly the productive activity that creates jobs and wealth. It's economically backwards—we tax labor (income tax), enterprise (business tax), and improvement (property tax on structures) while barely touching land speculation.

An LVT reverses these incentives. By taxing only land value while exempting improvements, it encourages development. Building doesn't increase your tax burden; leaving land vacant or underutilized does. This channels investment toward productive use rather than speculative holding.

In practice, this means more housing construction, more business development, and more intensive use of well-located land. Economic activity concentrates where it's most efficient—near transportation, services, and other economic opportunities—rather than scattering across the landscape in response to tax-distorted land prices.

Revenue Adequacy: Funding Government from Land Rent Alone

A common objection asks whether land rent could fund modern government. The evidence suggests it can—and comfortably so.

Land values represent enormous wealth. Estimates vary, but analyses suggest land represents 30-50% of total national wealth in developed countries. The annual rental value of this land—the income stream it generates—is substantial. Studies estimate that land rent comprises 20-30% of GDP in most developed nations, though this varies by country and methodology.

Consider that many governments already function on total revenues of 25-40% of GDP, much of which funds transfer payments that might be restructured under a Georgist system (more on this below). The public capture of land rent could plausibly replace most or all existing taxes, particularly when combined with modest reforms to expenditure priorities.

The Hidden Magnitude of Land Rent

Current statistics actually underestimate potential land rent revenue because existing taxes suppress land values. Property taxes on improvements reduce development incentives, decreasing land values below what they'd reach under an LVT-only system. Income and capital taxes reduce overall economic activity, similarly depressing land values.

Under a 100% LVT regime with no other taxes, economic activity would increase substantially. With labor, capital, and enterprise untaxed, productive activity would flourish. This would increase demand for well-located land, raising its rental value—and thus tax revenue—beyond current estimates.

Furthermore, the elimination of speculation and more efficient land use would concentrate economic activity geographically, further boosting location rents in productive areas. The revenue base would be not just adequate but robust.

International Evidence

Jurisdictions that have implemented even partial land value taxation demonstrate its revenue potential. Pennsylvania cities like Harrisburg and Pittsburgh have used split-rate taxation (higher rates on land than improvements) with notable success. Hong Kong, though not purely Georgist, funds substantial government operations through land leasing revenue, effectively capturing land rent.

Denmark, Estonia, and Singapore incorporate significant land value elements in their tax systems. Where implemented, these approaches have demonstrated reliable revenue generation without the economic damage of conventional taxation.

Admittedly, none of these cases represents a pure 100% LVT system, but they illustrate the principle's viability. The question is not whether land rent can fund government, but whether we have the political will to fully implement the most efficient and just tax system available.

Addressing Distribution and Equity

Beyond efficiency, a 100% LVT dramatically improves distributional equity by eliminating unearned privilege and reducing economic inequality.

Wealth Inequality and Land Ownership

Land ownership concentrates wealth. Those fortunate enough to own well-located land capture escalating values created by population growth and community development—wealth they didn't create. This mechanism perpetuates inequality across generations; those born into property ownership gain automatic claim to community-created wealth, while those without property must pay ever-increasing tributes for access to economic opportunity.

A 100% LVT eliminates this unearned privilege. Land still has private users, but they pay the full rental value to the community rather than to privileged titleholders. The community-created value returns to the community, available for public services, infrastructure, or citizen dividends.

This doesn't prevent individuals from becoming wealthy through productive effort. Those who create value through labor, innovation, or enterprise keep the fruits of their work entirely, untaxed. Only the appropriation of communal wealth through land monopoly ends.

Progressive Without Targeting

An LVT is inherently progressive without requiring complex means-testing or creating poverty traps. Land ownership correlates strongly with wealth; those who control valuable locations are generally better off than those who don't. Taxing land thus naturally falls on those most able to pay.

Moreover, land ownership is more concentrated than income. While many people earn wages, a smaller percentage controls significant land assets. Shifting tax burden from labor and enterprise to land therefore redistributes from the wealthy (disproportionate land owners) to ordinary workers and entrepreneurs.

Yet this progressivity emerges naturally from taxing privileged access to common resources, not from arbitrary redistribution. There's no moral hazard, no disincentive to work harder or become more productive. The system rewards creation while ending extraction.

The Citizen's Dividend

The revenue from a 100% LVT represents the community's collective wealth—the value created by our mutual presence and effort. One compelling approach would distribute this revenue, after funding essential services, as a universal citizen's dividend.

This achieves several goals: it ensures every person receives their equal share of natural resource value; it provides a basic economic foundation without welfare's stigma or means-testing complications; and it maintains the political sustainability of the system by making every citizen a direct beneficiary of public land rent collection.

Such a dividend would substantially reduce poverty and economic insecurity while preserving work incentives (since it's universal and unchanging regardless of income). Combined with untaxed wages making employment more attractive, this could virtually eliminate material deprivation.

Practical Implementation and Transition

Critics often concede the theoretical appeal of land value taxation while questioning its practical implementation. These concerns, though understandable, are surmountable.

Valuation Challenges

The most common technical objection involves separating land value from improvement value. This is indeed necessary for an LVT, but far from impossible. Property assessors already perform this separation, and modern computational tools, satellite imagery, and big data analytics make it increasingly precise.

Mass appraisal techniques can determine land values by comparing properties with different improvement levels in similar locations. Statistical modeling can isolate location value from structure value. In the digital age, these calculations become routine rather than challenging.

Moreover, unlike income or business taxation requiring intrusive examination of private affairs, land is visible and immobile. Assessment disputes involve observable property characteristics, not complex financial interpretations. This makes administration more transparent and less contentious than current tax systems.

Managing the Transition

The legitimate practical concern involves transition from current systems to a 100% LVT. Immediate implementation would create windfall gains and losses: those who recently purchased property at prices capitalized with low land taxes would face dramatic revaluations, while those who sold beforehand would escape the burden entirely.

This challenge requires thoughtful transition mechanisms, not abandonment of reform. A gradual phase-in over 10-20 years would allow adjustment, preventing catastrophic impacts on recent purchasers while steadily moving toward the efficient and just end state. Exemptions or deferrals for elderly homeowners or others who would face hardship could ease transitions for vulnerable groups.

The transition period will create winners and losers—this is unavoidable when correcting longstanding injustice. But the alternative is perpetuating an inefficient, inequitable system forever to protect those who happened to benefit from it. The ethical course is implementing reform with appropriate transition assistance, not abandoning justice to preserve accidental advantage.

Political Feasibility

The political challenge may exceed the technical one. Current landowners, particularly large holders of valuable urban land, benefit enormously from existing arrangements and will resist change. They are often politically influential, making reform difficult.

Yet history shows that fundamental tax reform is possible when circumstances align. The Progressive Era saw major restructuring of American taxation. Post-war periods have enabled significant policy shifts. Economic crises create political opportunities for reconsidering failed paradigms.

Moreover, a 100% LVT creates a powerful constituency: everyone who works, everyone who improves property, everyone frustrated by speculation-driven housing costs, everyone who pays income or sales tax. These groups vastly outnumber major landholders. The political challenge is organization and education, not inherent impossibility.

Answering Common Objections

"This would destroy property rights"

An LVT doesn't eliminate property rights in land; it properly defines them. Property rights have always included obligations, whether respecting others' boundaries or following zoning laws. An LVT simply recognizes that exclusive use of valuable locations creates an obligation to compensate the community for excluding others from that opportunity.

Moreover, true property rights protect what individuals create. Your right to your labor's fruits, your creative works, your built structures—these remain absolute under an LVT. Only the claim to capture community-created location value ends, and this was never a legitimate property right in the first place.

"Elderly homeowners would be forced from their homes"

This concern merits attention but doesn't justify abandoning reform. Several approaches address it: deferral programs allowing seniors to postpone payment until sale or inheritance; homestead exemptions for primary residences up to a certain value; or citizen dividends offsetting residential LVT obligations for modest properties.

More fundamentally, under an LVT regime, property prices would be dramatically lower (since capitalized land rent would disappear), making housing more affordable for the next generation. The transition challenges for current elderly owners, while real, must be weighed against perpetual housing unaffordability for the young.

"Businesses couldn't afford the tax on valuable commercial land"

Businesses using land productively would have no difficulty paying its rental value—they already do so, either explicitly through lease payments or implicitly through the opportunity cost of owned land. The LVT simply redirects this payment from private landlords to public revenue.

Businesses that cannot afford to pay market rent for their locations are by definition using land inefficiently—they value that location less than others would. An LVT ensures land flows to its highest-value uses, maximizing economic productivity. This might mean some businesses relocate to less expensive locations better suited to their needs, which is economically efficient.

"This is just socialism/communism"

This critique misunderstands both Georgism and socialism. Socialism advocates collective ownership of capital and means of production; Georgism fully protects private ownership of everything created by labor. A factory owner keeps their factory, a farmer keeps their crops, an inventor keeps their patent rights.

Georgism simply recognizes that land—which no one created—differs categorically from capital—which human effort produces. Taxing land rent no more constitutes socialism than charging for fishing licenses or mining rights. It's a public charge for exclusive use of common resources, fully compatible with market economics and private enterprise.

Indeed, by eliminating taxes on productive activity, an LVT creates a more genuinely capitalist system than our current arrangements, where government actively penalizes labor, enterprise, and improvement.

The Broader Vision: Economic and Social Transformation

Beyond specific technical advantages, a 100% LVT would catalyze profound positive transformation across multiple dimensions of society.

Urban Revitalization

Cities would densify organically around efficient transportation and infrastructure, ending sprawl's environmental and economic costs. Underutilized parcels in valuable locations would face development pressure, creating housing abundance that would crash artificially inflated prices. Homelessness—substantially driven by speculation-induced housing costs—would plummet.

Environmental Benefits

By ending incentives for sprawl, an LVT would preserve farmland and natural areas. Compact development reduces per-capita energy use, infrastructure costs, and carbon emissions. Most importantly, the same principle applies to natural resources beyond land: severance taxes on resource extraction (oil, minerals, etc.) and pollution charges represent Georgist principles extending to environmental protection.

A comprehensive system might tax not just location value but all resource use and pollution—appropriately pricing activities that impose costs on others. This would align private incentives with environmental sustainability far more effectively than our current approach of taxing productive work while allowing environmental degradation.

Economic Stability

Boom-bust cycles are substantially driven by land speculation. Easy credit fuels land price bubbles; their collapse triggers financial crises and recessions. By eliminating returns to speculation, an LVT would moderate these cycles, creating more stable economic growth.

With land values unable to bubble (since increases would flow to public revenue rather than speculator profits), financial system stability would improve dramatically. The 2008 crisis, like many previous crashes, centered on land-backed mortgage debt. A properly structured LVT regime would have prevented or dramatically softened that catastrophe.

Global Development

For developing nations, land value taxation offers particular promise. Many struggle with weak administrative capacity for complex tax systems; an LVT taxes a visible, immobile base that cannot be hidden. Corruption around land titles and zoning—major obstacles to development—becomes less lucrative when private land ownership confers no right to capture appreciation.

Resource-rich nations suffering the "resource curse" could fund development from resource rents rather than depending on external borrowing or distortionary taxation. This would align government incentives toward development rather than simple resource extraction.

Conclusion: The Moral Imperative

Henry George's question remains unanswerable by defenders of the status quo: "Why should those who do not labor be allowed to appropriate what labor produces?" Our current system permits exactly this injustice—those who contribute nothing to land's value capture its appreciation, while those who create wealth through actual productive effort face confiscatory taxation.

A 100% land value tax corrects this inversion. It ensures that those who create value keep what they create, while community-generated value returns to the community. It eliminates the inefficiency of conventional taxation while ending the injustice of private land rent capture. It makes housing affordable, development efficient, and prosperity broadly shared.

A Call to Justice: Reclaiming Our Common Birthright

My friends, we gather today to discuss not merely tax policy, but the fundamental question of economic justice that has plagued civilization since humans first drew boundaries in the soil.

The Great Injustice

Look around our cities. Who created the value of the land beneath Manhattan? Beneath London? Beneath any thriving community? Not the landlord. That value was created by all of us—by our presence, our labor, our infrastructure, our civilization itself. Yet who reaps the rewards? Those who hold the title deed and do nothing but wait for their check.

This is theft. Not the theft of what any person has made, but the theft of what we all have made together.

The Georgist Solution

Henry George saw this clearly over a century ago: Land is fundamentally different from all other property.

  • You can create a building—that's yours
  • You can create a business—that's yours
  • You can create art, invention, wealth—all yours

But no one created the land. No one created its location, its natural resources, its presence in a community. That value belongs to everyone equally—it is our common inheritance.

Therefore, we propose: Tax away 100% of the unimproved land value. Not the buildings. Not the improvements. Just the land itself—the location value created by society.

The Transformation

Imagine the world this creates:

For workers and entrepreneurs: No more income tax punishing your labor. No more sales tax discouraging commerce. No more taxes on the businesses you build or the homes you improve. Create value, and it's entirely yours.

Will we continue punishing work and innovation with taxes, while rewarding speculation and rent-seeking?

Or will we finally embrace the elegant solution that taxes nothing any person creates, but reclaims everything nature provides and society makes valuable?

The land belongs to all of us. Its rental value should fund the civilization that creates that value.

This is not confiscation—it is justice.

This is not radicalism—it is common sense.

This is not a tax—it is rent paid to the true owners: the community itself.

The time has come. The solution is clear. Let us have the courage to reclaim our common inheritance and build an economy where everyone keeps what they earn, and no one profits merely from owning what belongs to us all.

The land—and its value—belongs to the people!

Model Response:

A society that genuinely believes in fairness and efficiency should tax what nobody created and leave untaxed what everyone creates. That principle sits at the heart of Georgist economics and leads directly to a simple but radical proposal: abolish all conventional taxes and fund government entirely by a 100% land value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land—on the “location value” created by community and nature, not by individual effort.

Such a system would fully capture land rent for public benefit. It is fair because land value arises from nature and society, not the landowner’s labor. It is efficient because a land value tax does not distort productive decisions as taxes on work and capital do. And it is uniquely suited to serve as the sole source of government revenue because land is fixed in supply: it cannot flee, hide, or shrink in response to taxation. A 100% LVT would end land speculation, drastically reduce inequality, and liberate enterprise from the dead weight of conventional taxation.

Below is a detailed case for why a full land value tax is not only desirable but ethically compelling and economically superior.

I. What Is Being Taxed? The Distinction That Changes Everything

Land vs. Improvements

Georgism makes a crucial distinction between:

  • Land: the natural and locational qualities of sites—geography, access, infrastructure, surrounding population, legal protections, proximity to markets and amenities.
  • Improvements: buildings, machinery, crops, infrastructure built by human effort and capital.

A land value tax on the unimproved value of land means:

  • You pay tax based on what your site would be worth if it were a bare, vacant lot.
  • Your buildings, factories, homes, and other improvements are not taxed.

This distinction matters because the value of land is:

  • Not created by the landowner.
  • Created by nature, by the community, and by public investment.

When a downtown parcel is worth millions while identical soil at the edge of the desert is worth almost nothing, that value difference is not due to the landowner, but to:

  • Population density.
  • Nearby businesses and customers.
  • Public infrastructure (roads, transit, utilities).
  • Public safety, schools, environmental quality.
  • Legal stability and property rights.

These are social and public contributions that crystallize into location value, which is what Georgists call economic rent of land.

A land value tax simply recaptures this socially created value for social use.

II. The Moral Case: Why Fully Capturing Land Rent Is Fair

1. Landownership as Privilege, Not Productive Contribution

Unlike a carpenter who makes furniture or an engineer who designs software, a landowner contributes nothing essential to the existence of land. Ownership is a legal grant, not a productive act.

Yet landowners receive enormous, effortless income in the form of rising land values:

  • They purchase land once.
  • Public investment and private development around them increase its value.
  • They capture higher rents and capital gains without doing anything.

This is unearned income derived from exclusive control over a natural and social asset. If someone owns the only spring in a desert and charges others access, they are not creating water—they are monetizing their legal privilege.

Georgism views this as fundamentally unjust:

  • People should keep the full fruits of their labor.
  • But no one has a moral claim to the unearned economic rent of nature and location.

2. The Principle of Equal Right to the Earth

Every person, by mere existence, needs access to land to live: to stand, to build, to grow food, to work. If land is monopolized—held unused or underused—others are denied opportunities and must pay tribute in the form of rent.

The Georgist principle is: > The earth is the common inheritance of all. Exclusive use is permissible only if the user compensates everyone else for excluding them.

A 100% land value tax operationalizes this:

  • You may have exclusive use of a site.
  • But you pay the full annual land rental value to the community.
  • The community is compensated for the opportunity cost of being excluded from that location.

This is analogous to paying a fee to use a public resource:

  • We accept it as fair that companies pay for mining rights, radio spectrum, or fishing quotas.
  • Land is even more fundamental; its use should similarly require compensating society.

3. Removing the Unearned Advantage of Birth or Purchase

In a system without LVT:

  • The children of landowners inherit valuable urban and agricultural land.
  • The children of landless families inherit nothing but the obligation to pay rent.

This perpetuates inequality based not on effort, but on birth. A 100% LVT:

  • Severely limits the ability to live off rentier income.
  • Ensures that wealth comes primarily from labor, skill, and innovation rather than from owning location.
  • Makes inheritance of land more like inheriting a lease: the right to use, not the right to extract unearned gains forever.

It does not abolish private property in land; it abolishes private appropriation of land’s economic rent, which morally belongs to everyone.

III. The Economic Case: Why Land Value Taxation Is Uniquely Efficient

1. Land Is Fixed in Supply: Taxing It Does Not Reduce It

Most taxes distort behavior:

  • Tax labor, and people work less or move away.
  • Tax buildings, and builders invest less.
  • Tax capital gains, and investors divert capital into tax shelters.
  • Tax sales, and consumption patterns change.

These distortions cause what economists call deadweight loss: lost economic value purely due to the tax.

Land is different:

  • Its quantity is fixed.
  • It cannot be moved offshore.
  • It cannot be hidden in a spreadsheet.
  • It cannot be “produced less” in response to taxation.

Since the supply of land is perfectly inelastic, a tax on land value:

  • Does not shrink the amount of land available.
  • Does not deter its “production” (because it’s not produced by humans).
  • Simply transfers income from private landowners to the public.

Modern economic consensus broadly recognizes that a tax on:

  • True land value (not on buildings),
  • At the correct assessed value,
  • Is among the least distortionary—arguably the most efficient—taxes.

A 100% LVT takes this logic to its natural conclusion: if we must tax something, tax only that which cannot be distorted or reduced—land rent.

2. Encouraging Optimal Land Use and Ending Speculation

When land is lightly taxed or untaxed:

  • Owners can afford to hold valuable sites vacant or underused while they wait for prices to rise.
  • This is pure land speculation: betting on future community development without contributing to it.
  • Speculation leads to urban sprawl, housing shortages, and wasted infrastructure.

A high or full land value tax changes incentives dramatically:

  • Owners must pay the annual land value whether they build or not.
  • Holding land idle becomes expensive.
  • The only way to cover the tax and profit is to use land efficiently: building housing, businesses, or other productive improvements.

Consequences:

  • Vacant lots in city centers get developed.
  • Parking lots on prime sites are replaced by taller mixed-use buildings.
  • Speculators selling “future potential” lose ground to actual builders and entrepreneurs.
  • Urban land is used intensely and efficiently, reducing sprawl and infrastructure costs.

In effect, a 100% LVT punishes land hoarding and rewards development.

3. Unburdening Labor and Capital: A True Free Market for Productivity

Current tax systems undermine productive activity:

  • Income taxes discourage working more or formal employment.
  • Payroll taxes raise the cost of hiring employees.
  • Corporate taxes disincentivize investment and scaling.
  • Sales and value-added taxes discourage consumption and trade.
  • Property taxes on buildings penalize improvements and maintenance.

By contrast, a pure land value tax:

  • Removes taxes on labor: wages are untaxed; people keep all earnings from work.
  • Removes taxes on capital: businesses and investors keep full returns on productive investment.
  • Removes taxes on transactions and enterprise: no taxes on sales, profits, or innovation.

This unleashes a genuinely free market in:

  • Human effort.
  • Capital investment.
  • Entrepreneurship.

People can:

  • Move jobs or start businesses without worrying about punitive tax brackets.
  • Improve their properties without facing higher taxes on the buildings themselves.
  • Innovate, invest, and trade without the friction of tax codes and compliance overhead.

Georgism is not anti-market; it is pro-market:

  • It insists that markets should be free where value is created by human action.
  • And that the economic rent of natural monopolies—land and similar resources—should go to everyone.

IV. Why 100% LVT Should Be the Sole Source of Government Revenue

1. Land Rent Is Large Enough to Fund Government

In modern economies, the annual rental value of land is enormous:

  • Urban land values in major cities amount to trillions of dollars.
  • Agricultural land, mineral rights, water access, and other natural-site values add further trillions.
  • Real estate markets show that land values often exceed the value of structures.

When properly assessed:

  • The total land rent (what land could earn in an open market if rented) is sufficient, in many cases, to fund a large portion or even the entirety of government budgets.

Moreover:

  • When other taxes are removed, economic activity increases; productivity and GDP rise.
  • Higher productivity and better urban use make land more valuable, raising land rent further.
  • Thus, the tax base grows dynamically as the economy is freed from distortionary taxes.

The Georgist vision is:

  • A government funded entirely by land rent.
  • No taxes on earnings, sales, trade, buildings, or capital.
  • A simple and transparent system where the public recovers the natural value of its shared environment.

2. Simplicity, Transparency, and Reduced Administrative Burden

A single-source revenue system has profound advantages:

  • Simplicity: No sprawling tax codes divided among income, corporate profits, consumption, inheritance, capital gains, etc.
  • Transparency: Citizens know exactly how public revenue is raised: from land rent.
  • Reduced compliance costs: Individuals and businesses no longer need expensive tax planning and complex reporting.
  • Less corruption and loopholes: Fewer opportunities to manipulate classifications, deductions, and exemptions.

Assessment of land value, while requiring competence, is:

  • Fundamentally more stable than tracking global income flows.
  • Based on observable market transactions and professional appraisal methods.
  • More resistant to evasion: you cannot hide a city block or relocate it to a tax haven.

Where today governments chase income and profit across borders, under a pure LVT:

  • The tax base is immovable.
  • Enforcement is simpler.
  • The system is more robust to globalization and financial engineering.

3. Aligning Public Finance with Public Contribution

Currently:

  • Government builds infrastructure and improves public services.
  • These investments raise nearby land values.
  • But the extra value is privatized by landowners who did not fund the infrastructure.

Under a 100% LVT:

  • When government invests in a new transit line, park, or school, nearby land values rise.
  • That increase in value comes back directly as higher land tax revenue.
  • The very areas benefiting most from public investment automatically fund it.

This creates:

  • A self-correcting feedback loop:
    • If a project raises land values substantially, the cost is justified by increased LVT.
    • If a project fails to raise land values, it is financially self-limiting.
  • A discipline on public spending: governments are incentivized to invest where they truly improve the public realm.

Revenue and expenditure become tightly linked:

  • The community invests in itself.
  • The resulting increase in land rent finances ongoing improvements.

V. Addressing Common Objections

Objection 1: “A 100% LVT Confiscates Property and Destroys Incentives”

A 100% land value tax is often misunderstood as confiscation. This is incorrect.

Distinctions:

  • It taxes the site value, not buildings, crops, or machinery.
  • It does not prevent ownership; it conditions ownership on paying the full annual rental value.
  • It does not confiscate improvements; it encourages them by not taxing them.

Owners still have:

  • Security of tenure as long as they pay the tax.
  • Full control over how they use and improve the site.
  • Full private benefit from their improvements.

Their incentive:

  • To make the land as productive as possible to cover the tax and earn profit.

What is removed is only the ability to collect unearned rent from location value, which is not their creation.

Objection 2: “But Some Landowners Bought Land Fairly—Isn’t It Unjust to Change the System?”

Buying land under the current rules does not create an eternal moral right to unearned rent:

  • People who bought monopoly rights or slave ownership under past laws did so “fairly” within those systems, but that did not justify perpetuating the underlying injustice.

A fair transition can:

  • Phase in LVT gradually to avoid shock.
  • Offer limited compensation or tax credits to those who recently purchased land at high prices under the old regime.
  • Reduce other taxes in step with rising LVT, so overall burden isn’t increased suddenly.

But the underlying principle stands:

  • The past existence of a privilege does not justify its perpetuation when it is recognized as unjust.

Objection 3: “Land Value Is Hard to Assess Accurately”

Actually:

  • Markets for land exist everywhere.
  • Appraisal professions and methods are well developed.
  • Many jurisdictions already separate land and improvement values for property tax purposes.

Improving assessment:

  • Use mass appraisal techniques, GIS data, and machine learning to refine estimates.
  • Regularly update values based on transactions.
  • Allow appeals and transparent methodologies.

Even imperfect assessments can be better than the current system:

  • Income and corporate tax enforcement are riddled with complexity and evasion.
  • LVT, while not perfect, is simpler and more grounded in observable prices.

Moreover:

  • The goal is not mathematical perfection but relative accuracy sufficient to capture most rent and shape incentives correctly.
  • As practice improves, so will precision.

Objection 4: “What About Non-Land Natural Resources and Monopolies?”

A strict Georgist system extends the principle:

  • Tax economic rent from all natural resources: oil, minerals, water, fisheries, the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Where private monopolies exist due to public franchise (utilities, railroads), regulate them or capture their monopoly rent through fees.

But crucially:

  • The unimproved value of land is the largest and most universal base.
  • If some societies wish to fund additional functions, they can extend rent-capture to other forms of natural or legally created monopoly.

The ethical core remains:

  • Capture rent from what no individual created.
  • Leave untaxed what individuals create through labor and capital.

VI. Social and Political Benefits

1. Dramatically Reducing Inequality

The biggest fortunes in many countries are rooted in land and natural resources:

  • Urban real estate empires.
  • Agricultural estates.
  • Mining and oil concessions.

A full LVT:

  • Breaks the power of rentier wealth.
  • Forces landholders to contribute to public revenue proportionally to the location value they control.
  • Channels what is now private rent into public benefit, which can be:
    • Universal public services.
    • A citizen dividend (basic income funded from land rent).
    • Lower or zero taxes on work and business.

This transforms wealth dynamics:

  • Opportunities for wealth become tied to effort and innovation, not mere ownership.
  • The floor of living standards can be raised through public revenue from land rent.
  • The ceiling is not artificially amplified by unearned appreciation of land.

2. Stable, Affordable Housing and Urban Livability

Housing crises in major cities are often driven by:

  • Land speculation.
  • Holding sites vacant or underused.
  • Restrictive development patterns.

A strong LVT:

  • Makes it costly to sit on prime land without building housing.
  • Encourages higher-density, mixed-use development in central areas.
  • Reduces pressure to expand endlessly into suburbs and exurbs.

Consequences:

  • More housing supply in desirable locations.
  • Lower land costs passed through to lower rents and purchase prices.
  • More walkable, transit-oriented cities with better use of infrastructure.

3. Less Political Rent-Seeking

When land rent is publicly captured:

  • The incentive for lobbying to secure land-related favors is reduced.
  • Politicians cannot grant lucrative land windfalls if those windfalls are taxed away.
  • Economic power that buys political influence is less rooted in passive ownership.

Politics can focus more on:

  • How to best use public revenue for common benefit.
  • How to improve public services and infrastructure.
  • Competing visions of social investment, instead of competing for special deals.

VII. The Georgist Vision: Freedom, Justice, and Prosperity Together

Georgist economics offers a synthesis that many ideologies fail to achieve:

  • From liberalism and libertarianism:

    • Respect for private property in the products of labor.
    • Desire for free markets and minimal distortion.
    • Opposition to taxing productive effort.

  • From socialism and egalitarian thought:

    • Recognition that natural resources and the environment are a common inheritance.
    • Need to prevent unearned, extractive wealth based on monopoly.
    • Commitment to social justice and opportunity for all.

A 100% land value tax, as the sole source of government revenue, expresses this synthesis in concrete policy:

  • It preserves and strengthens markets where they work: in labor and capital.
  • It socializes the rent of land and natural monopolies, where markets fail due to exclusivity over common resources.
  • It dramatically simplifies taxation, aligns incentives, and makes public finance morally coherent.

Conclusion: Why We Should Fully Embrace Land Value Taxation

Capturing the full land rent through a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, and using it as the sole source of government revenue, is not a utopian fantasy. It is a clear, principled response to long-standing injustices and inefficiencies embedded in our treatment of land.

It is fair because:

  • Land’s value is created by nature and community, not by the owner.
  • Exclusive use rightly requires compensating everyone else.
  • It restores equal rights to the earth while preserving private use and improvement.

It is efficient because:

  • Taxing land does not distort supply or productive behavior.
  • It ends speculative holding and promotes optimal land use.
  • It liberates labor and capital from distortionary taxes, expanding productive capacity.

It is practical as a sole revenue source because:

  • Aggregate land rent is large and grows as the economy is freed.
  • It simplifies public finance, cuts compliance costs, and reduces evasion.
  • It automatically aligns public investment with community benefit.

In a world facing inequality, housing crises, overcomplex tax systems, and underused urban spaces, a full land value tax offers a powerful, coherent solution. It does not ask people to sacrifice prosperity for justice; it shows that justice in how we treat land is the precondition for lasting prosperity.

If we truly believe that people should own what they create, and that no one should own the earth at others’ expense, then funding government solely by a 100% tax on land’s unimproved value is not merely an elegant idea—it is an ethical imperative.

1. Land value is socially created, not individually produced

Land (in the economic sense) is not produced by humans. Its value comes from:

  • Natural qualities (fertility, mineral deposits, climate, location on a coast or river)

  • General economic activity (business clusters, job opportunities, cultural life)

Therefore:

  • What we call “land value” or “site value” is mostly a social product, not the result of the owner’s personal effort or investment.

2. Distinguishing “unimproved land value” from improvements

Georgism draws a sharp line between:

  • Unimproved land value – the market value of a bare site, excluding buildings or other human-made improvements.
  • Improvements/capital – structures, drainage, grading beyond what is legally required, crops, machinery, etc.

The tax they propose falls only on the unimproved value of the site, not on anything the owner builds or creates. Reasons:

We stand at a crossroads.

On one side is the world we know all too well: soaring land prices, crushing rents, speculative bubbles, and people working harder every year just to stand still. Fund government entirely through a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land.
End private land rent.
Free labor and capital from all other taxes.

We are not talking about taxing your labor.
We are not talking about taxing your business, your savings, your buildings, your machinery, your creativity, or your effort.
We are talking about reclaiming for the public what the public itself creates: the value of location, of community, of infrastructure, of nature’s gifts.

Unimproved land value is not produced by the individual owner.
The value of a downtown lot does not arise from the will of a landlord; it arises from the people: from the businesses that cluster nearby, from the public transit lines, from the schools and parks, from the safety provided by public institutions, from the very presence of millions of others who want to live and work there.

Rent, in the economic sense, is payment for permission—to stand, to live, to build—on a piece of the Earth. When that payment goes to a private owner who did nothing to create the land and did not create the surrounding community, it is not a reward for productive contribution. It is a toll on existence.

Every month, millions pay this toll:
• The renter handing over half their paycheck for a cramped apartment.
• The small business struggling to keep the doors open as commercial rent soars.
• The young family locked out of the housing market because land speculation has driven prices beyond reach.

These are not natural laws. They are policy choices.

We tax what we say we disapprove of. Today, our governments heavily tax labor, enterprise, and trade. We tax wages when people work. We tax profits when businesses succeed. We tax sales when people buy and sell.

Then we turn around and barely tax—if at all—the passive appropriation of land value, a value produced by all of us.
We punish work. We reward mere ownership.

This is backward. It is unjust. And it is economically destructive.

A 100% tax on unimproved land value—on the rental value of the bare site, ignoring buildings and improvements—would reverse this perverse logic.

First, it is just.

Land, unlike anything else, is not created by human effort. No one made the Earth. No one produced the continents or the minerals, the rivers or the coastlines, the fertile plains or the urban locations. The titles we hold are not claims to what we built; they are legal permissions, granted by society, to control access to a piece of the planet.

If the community grants that legal privilege, why should the community not take back, in full, the economic value arising from it?

Speculation withers.
Vacant lots in thriving downtowns become too costly to sit on.
Housing supply increases as underused land is developed.
Business opportunities expand as land is used productively instead of warehoused for future gain.

Third, it is transformative.

Imagine a world where every other tax on productive activity is gone or drastically reduced because government is funded by capturing the full rental value of land.

No more income tax biting into your paycheck.
No more payroll taxes making every job more expensive to create.
No more sales tax burdening everyday purchases.
No more taxes on buildings that deter construction and renovation.

Instead, the public budget—schools, hospitals, infrastructure, environmental protection—is financed by the value of our shared land, collected transparently and predictably.

Put a small house or a skyscraper on your lot—the tax is unchanged, because it is tied to the value of the land itself, which the community creates.

This is not bureaucrats telling you what to do.
It is the liberation of markets from a deeply entrenched, feudal relic: the private appropriation of land rent.

Courage to say that no one, however wealthy or connected, has a rightful claim to extract unearned rent from the community forever.
Courage to confront a structure of privilege that hides behind the language of “investment” while living off the toil of others.
Courage to reimagine public finance from the ground up, rooted in justice.

• No more private windfalls from rising land prices that others created.
• No more speculative hoarding of prime sites while workers commute hours from the fringes.
• No more punishing taxes on work, trade, and enterprise.
• A stable, immovable tax base that cannot flee offshore or disappear in accounting games.
• A powerful, permanent incentive to use land efficiently, sustainably, and humanely.

When you hold a piece of land under this system, you hold a clear responsibility: pay the community the full rental value for this privilege, or relinquish it to someone who will. Within that framework, you are free—free to build, to innovate, to live.

Where public transit and parks are funded not by squeezing wages, but by the very land they enrich. Where entrepreneurship flourishes because starting a business no longer means navigating a thicket of punitive taxes.

A 100% tax on unimproved land value is a call to align our laws with that deeper understanding of freedom and justice.

Let us have the honesty to recognize that much of what we call “property income” from land is, in fact, legalized tribute. And let us have the resolve to end it—not by tearing down what people build, but by reclaiming what no one built: the land itself and the value that arises from our shared life upon it.

We are not fighting against markets; we are fighting against monopoly.
We are not attacking property; we are defining it correctly.
We are not undermining prosperity; we are laying its strongest possible foundation.

This is the path:
• Tax away 100% of land’s unimproved rental value.
• Abolish private land rent as a source of private income.
• Use that revenue to fund all essential public services, and to lift the burden of taxation from work and enterprise.

Let us choose a tax system that reflects our highest principles, not our oldest injustices.

This is our moment to say: the Earth is for all of us, and the value that arises from our being together on it shall serve all of us.

Let us have the courage to take that step.
