Georgist Economic Philosophy and the “Single Tax” on Unimproved Land Value

Georgism, named after the 19th‑century American economist Henry George, is a school of thought that argues that the value of land (the natural resource) is a form of economic rent that belongs to society as a whole. The central policy prescription of Georgism is the land value tax (LVT)—a tax levied on the unimproved value of land, i.e., the value of the site itself, independent of any buildings, improvements, or other human‑made structures. Proponents of Georgism advocate that this tax should be the sole source of public revenue, replacing all other taxes (income, sales, corporate, etc.). Below is a factual, step‑by‑step explanation of the supposed benefits and reasons behind this proposal.

1. Core Concept: Land as a Unique Factor of Production

  • Land is a fixed, non‑reproducible resource. Unlike labor or capital, the total supply of land cannot be increased. Its value derives from its location, natural fertility, and proximity to infrastructure, not from the effort of the owner.
  • Land rent is “unearned.” Because land is not produced by anyone, the income derived from owning land (the “economic rent”) is considered a surplus that accrues to the owner simply by virtue of ownership, not through productive effort.
  • Land value is socially created. The value of a plot of land is largely determined by public investments (roads, schools, police, utilities) and the surrounding community, not by the landowner’s actions.

2. Why Tax Only Unimproved Land Value?

  • Avoids discouraging productive activity. A tax on the value of the land itself does not penalize the owner for building, farming, or otherwise using the land productively. In contrast, taxes on income, profits, or consumption can reduce incentives to work, invest, or innovate.
  • No deadweight loss. Economic theory suggests that a tax on a fixed, inelastic resource (land) does not distort market behavior; it merely captures a portion of the rent that would otherwise accrue to the owner. This is why Georgists claim the LVT is “efficient.”
  • Simplicity and transparency. Land values can be assessed relatively easily (through market data, cadastral maps, and valuation models), making the tax administratively straightforward compared to complex income or corporate tax codes.

3. Supposed Benefits of a 100% Land Value Tax as the Sole Revenue Source

Benefit Explanation
Economic efficiency By taxing only the unearned rent, the tax does not discourage productive use of land. Owners have no incentive to leave land idle; they must either use it productively or sell it to someone who will. This reduces “land hoarding” and speculative bubbles.
Elimination of land speculation High land values often result from expectations of future price increases, not current productive use. A high LVT reduces the profitability of buying land solely to resell later, encouraging development and reducing price volatility.
Promotes optimal land use Landowners face a cost for holding land idle, so they are motivated to develop, rent, or sell it. This can lead to more efficient allocation of urban and rural land, reducing sprawl and encouraging compact, mixed‑use development.
Reduces inequality Land ownership is highly concentrated (a small share of the population owns a large share of land value). A tax that captures this rent is inherently progressive: the wealthy, who own most land, pay a larger share of revenue.
Funds public services without distortion Since the tax does not affect labor or capital, it can finance government functions (infrastructure, education, public safety) without creating disincentives for work or investment.
Simplifies the tax system Replacing multiple taxes with a single land tax reduces compliance costs, administrative overhead, and opportunities for tax avoidance or evasion.
Encourages investment in improvements Because the tax is based on the unimproved value, owners are not penalized for adding buildings, farms, or other improvements. This can stimulate construction and capital formation.
Reduces poverty and homelessness By making land more affordable (through reduced speculation and lower holding costs), the tax can expand access to housing and productive land, potentially alleviating poverty.
Moral and ethical appeal Georgists argue that since land is a common heritage, the community should capture the rent it generates, ensuring that the benefits of public investment are shared rather than monopolized by private owners.

4. Reasons for Adopting the LVT as the Sole Source of Revenue

  1. The “single tax” principle – Henry George argued that all other taxes (income, sales, corporate) are unjust because they tax productive effort. By replacing them with a tax on land rent, the system becomes “just” and “efficient.”
  2. Elimination of tax distortions – Income and consumption taxes create deadweight losses by discouraging work and consumption. A land tax avoids these distortions, allowing the market to allocate labor and capital efficiently.
  3. Funding public goods without hidden costs – Public services (roads, schools, police) increase land values. A land tax captures the value created by these services, ensuring that the beneficiaries (landowners) pay for them directly.
  4. Moral claim of common ownership – Georgists hold that land is a natural resource that belongs to everyone. Taxing its value returns that value to the community, rather than allowing private owners to appropriate it.
  5. Economic rent is a surplus – Because land is not produced, the rent it generates is a surplus that can be taxed without harming the economy. The “100%” figure is a theoretical ideal; in practice, rates are set high (often 50–100% of the annual land rent) to capture most of this surplus.

5. Practical Considerations and Common Criticisms

  • Implementation challenges – Accurately assessing land values, especially in areas with limited market data, can be difficult. Political resistance from powerful landowners is also common.
  • Transition effects – A sudden shift to a 100% LVT could cause short‑term disruptions, especially for owners who rely on land as a primary asset.
  • Revenue sufficiency – Critics argue that a land tax alone may not generate enough revenue to fund all government functions, especially in large, complex economies.
  • Equity concerns – While the tax is progressive in theory, low‑income homeowners (who may own land but have limited cash flow) could face hardship if the tax is not structured with exemptions or payment plans.
  • Political feasibility – The idea of eliminating all other taxes is radical and faces opposition from entrenched interests that benefit from the current tax system.

6. Summary

Georgist philosophy proposes a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land as the sole source of public revenue because:

  • Land is a fixed, socially created resource whose value is largely unearned.
  • Taxing land rent does not discourage productive activity, making it economically efficient.
  • It eliminates speculation, promotes optimal land use, and reduces inequality.
  • It simplifies the tax system and funds public services without distorting incentives.
  • It aligns with the moral principle that land belongs to the community, not to private owners.

The Unearned Increment: Why a 100% Land Value Tax is the Moral and Economic Foundation of a Just Society

The first and most compelling argument for a 100% LVT is its unassailable moral foundation. All other major forms of taxation are fundamentally a punishment of human effort and ingenuity. An income tax confiscates a portion of a person’s labor; a sales tax penalizes the act of exchange; a corporate tax stifles entrepreneurial risk-taking. The value of a vacant lot in midtown Manhattan does not stem from anything its owner has done; it stems entirely from the collective presence of millions of people, from public infrastructure like subways and sewers, and from the agglomeration of commerce and culture that the community has built over centuries. The 100% LVT rectifies this by returning the rental value of land, which rightfully belongs to the entire community, back to the community that created it. It is the fiscal expression of the principle that what an individual creates, they should keep, and what society creates, society should collect.

Beyond its moral justice, the 100% LVT is a powerhouse of economic efficiency that would demolish the deadweight losses crippling modern economies. The current tax system is a labyrinth of perverse incentives. Taxing labor discourages work; taxing capital discourages investment; taxing buildings discourages construction and improvement. A pure, full LVT has no such disincentive. The supply of land is perfectly inelastic—it cannot be created or destroyed. Taxing it at 100% of its potential annual rental value does not cause the land to shrink or flee the jurisdiction. The tax cannot be passed on to tenants, because the supply of land remains fixed, and market rents are determined by what people are willing to pay, not by the landlord’s tax bill. Instead, the tax falls entirely on the landowner, effectively reducing the private selling price of land to zero or near zero while its annual rental value becomes the public revenue.

This mechanism transforms land from a speculative commodity into a productive asset that must be used. The tax burden is shifted from the producer to the passive rent-collector, turning real estate from a vehicle for extraction into a conduit for public revenue.

If the community’s collective presence and public spending are precisely what give land its value, then the total rental value of all land within a jurisdiction represents a perfectly correlated, natural, and self-liquidating fund for public expenses. Every dollar of public money spent on a new transit line, a park, a school, or a water system is capitalized directly into the land values surrounding it. With a 100% LVT, this process forms a perfect feedback loop. It is a self-funding, virtuous cycle of public investment. The immense pool of credit currently fueling speculative booms and devastating busts would be redirected to where it can actually grow the economy, not just inflate an asset bubble.

It is the only form of taxation that is morally sound, because it reclaims what the community creates rather than seizing what the individual produces. It is uniquely efficient, because it cannot be shifted, it punishes no productive activity, and it forces idle land into use. A 100 % Land‑Value Tax on Unimproved Land: The Georgist Prescription for a Fair, Efficient, and Sustainable Public Treasury

By [Your Name]

Introduction

Imagine a tax system that eliminates the distortions of every other levy, that removes the incentive to hoard or misuse land, and that supplies the government with a steady, predictable stream of revenue without ever penalising productive activity. This is not a utopian fantasy; it is the logical outcome of a 100 % land‑value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land, a policy rooted in the economic insights of Henry George and refined by generations of scholars.

In this essay I will argue, in three inter‑locking stages, that a full‑rate LVT is fair because it captures a rent that belongs to the community, efficient because it eliminates economic deadweight loss and spurs optimal use of scarce resources, and sufficient because it can, by itself, fund all legitimate public functions. The case rests on three pillars: (1) the nature of land rent as a pure economic surplus, (2) the distortion‑free character of a land‑value tax, and (3) the empirical and theoretical evidence that a properly calibrated LVT can meet modern fiscal needs.

1. The Moral Foundations: Land Rent Belongs to All

1.1. Land as a Unique Factor of Production

Unlike labor, capital, or entrepreneurship, land cannot be produced, stored, or improved by its owner. Its value is generated by three forces that lie outside the individual’s control:

  1. Location – proximity to markets, infrastructure, schools, and natural amenities.
  2. Community Investment – roads, parks, police protection, and public services that raise the desirability of a place.
  3. Scarcity – the finite supply of any given parcel in a given location.

Because these determinants are socially created, the economic rent that accrues to a landowner is a gift of the community. Henry George famously wrote, “The ground on which we stand is a common inheritance; its value is a common wealth.”

1.2. The Principle of “Economic Rent”

Economic rent is defined as the payment to a factor of production in excess of what is needed to keep it in its current use. For land, the “cost of supply” is zero; the owner does not need any compensation to keep the land where it is, because the land cannot be moved or replicated. Consequently, all of the market price of land is rent.

When a private individual captures this rent, they are extracting a portion of the community’s collective investment without contributing back. This creates a moral imbalance: the public pays for the roads, schools, and security that make the land valuable, yet the private owner reaps the financial reward. A 100 % LVT restores the rightful balance by returning the entire surplus to the public purse.

1.3. Fairness in the Modern Context

In contemporary economies, the share of national wealth that is land‑based has risen dramatically because of urbanisation, zoning restrictions, and speculative bubbles. The resulting wealth concentration is a direct consequence of private capture of land rent. A full LVT would:

  • Reduce wealth inequality by limiting the ability of a few to amass fortunes solely through location advantage.
  • Promote inter‑generational equity because the tax does not penalise future generations for the productive use of land; it merely recovers the community‑generated surplus.
  • Align with progressive taxation principles: the tax burden rises automatically with the value of the land, which is highly correlated with income and wealth, yet it does not penalise effort or innovation.

2. Economic Efficiency: The LVT Is the Only Non‑Distortionary Tax

2.1. The “Diamond‑Mountif” Insight

In 1975, economists Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees proved that a tax on land value is the only tax that can be levied without creating deadweight loss. The logic is simple: because the supply of land is perfectly inelastic, any tax on its value does not change the quantity supplied. The market simply passes the tax onto the price, leaving the allocation of resources untouched.

2.2. Eliminating Distortions in Other Tax Bases

All other taxes—on labor, consumption, capital gains, or corporate profits—alter behaviour:

  • Labor taxes discourage work and reduce hours supplied.
  • Consumption taxes discourage spending, slowing aggregate demand.
  • Capital taxes deter investment, stifling innovation and long‑run growth.

By replacing these distortionary taxes with a full LVT, we remove the wedge between private incentives and social optimum. The result is a Pareto‑improving reallocation of resources: workers keep more of their earnings, firms retain more profit for reinvestment, and consumers face lower prices.

2.3. Land‑Use Efficiency and Urban Form

A 100 % LVT directly addresses the chronic problem of under‑utilised land—the “urban sprawl” that forces commuters to travel longer distances, inflates infrastructure costs, and harms the environment. When landowners must pay the full market rent, they are incentivised to:

  • Develop vacant or under‑used parcels rather than holding them idle for speculative gain.
  • Build higher‑density, mixed‑use projects that maximise the value per square metre.
  • Relocate or sell land that cannot be profitably developed, freeing it for more productive uses.

Empirical studies from cities that have implemented partial land‑value taxes (e.g., Pittsburgh, Harrisburg, and parts of Singapore) show significant reductions in vacant lots, higher construction rates, and lower housing price volatility. A full LVT would amplify these effects, resulting in more compact, walkable, and environmentally sustainable cities.

3. Fiscal Sufficiency: A Single Tax Can Fund All Legitimate Government Functions

3.1. Revenue Potential

The total annual land‑value rent in a mature economy is enormous. In the United States, estimates of the gross land rent (including both urban and rural parcels) range from $2.5 trillion to $4 trillion per year—roughly 15–25 % of GDP. Even a conservative capture of 50 % would already exceed the current federal budget (≈$4.8 trillion). A 100 % LVT would therefore provide a revenue surplus that can be used to:

  • Fund core public services (education, health, national defence).
  • Replace regressive taxes (sales taxes, payroll taxes) that disproportionately burden low‑income households.
  • Finance infrastructure that, in turn, raises land values, creating a virtuous feedback loop.

3.2. Stability and Predictability

Land values are relatively stable over short horizons because they are anchored in location and community amenities, not in volatile market cycles. This stability translates into a predictable revenue stream, reducing the need for ad‑hoc fiscal adjustments and the political uncertainty associated with annual budget negotiations.

3.3. Administrative Simplicity

A single, uniform tax on a clearly defined asset eliminates the complexity and compliance costs of a multi‑tax system. Modern GIS and property‑assessment technologies allow for real‑time, high‑resolution valuation of every parcel, ensuring transparency and minimizing opportunities for evasion.

3.4. The “Fiscal‑Neutrality” Argument

Critics often claim that a land‑value tax would be insufficient to fund modern welfare states. However, the fiscal‑neutrality principle demonstrates that any revenue requirement can be met by adjusting the tax rate on land. Because the tax base is elastic in price (the market price of land rises when the tax is increased), the government can raise the rate until the desired revenue is reached, without ever harming economic efficiency.

4. Addressing Common Objections

Objection Rebuttal
“Land owners will be forced into bankruptcy.” The tax is non‑distortionary; owners who are already using the land productively will retain the surplus after paying the rent. Those holding land idle will be compelled to either develop or sell it, which is socially beneficial.
“It will discourage investment in improvements.” The tax is levied only on the unimproved value. Any investment in buildings, infrastructure, or landscaping is exempt and therefore fully rewarded. This encourages private improvement while recapturing the community‑generated component.
“Valuation is difficult and prone to error.” Modern cadastral systems, satellite imagery, and machine‑learning valuation models provide high‑precision assessments. Moreover, the tax can be phased in with a transparent appeals process to build confidence.
“It will cause massive capital flight.” Because land is non‑mobile, the tax cannot be avoided by moving assets abroad. Only the unimproved value is taxed, so owners retain full rights to the structures and businesses they build.
“It is politically impossible.” Historically, partial LVTs have been implemented successfully (e.g., Hong Kong’s “rate” system). A well‑communicated narrative—emphasising fairness, efficiency, and environmental benefits—can win broad public support, especially when paired with a tax‑reform package that eliminates other regressive taxes.

5. Implementation Roadmap

  1. Comprehensive Land‑Value Assessment – Use existing cadastral data, augment with GIS and AI‑driven valuation, and publish a public register of land values.
  2. Gradual Phase‑In – Start with a 50 % LVT on a pilot region (e.g., a major metropolitan area) while simultaneously reducing other taxes. Monitor revenue, land‑use changes, and economic indicators.
  3. Full‑Rate Adoption – Once the system proves stable, expand to 100 % nationwide, accompanied by a tax‑swap that eliminates income, sales, and corporate taxes.
  4. Revenue Allocation – Direct a fixed proportion of LVT revenue to a public‑investment fund for infrastructure, affordable housing, and climate‑resilient projects. The remainder funds the core budget.
  5. Legal Framework – Enact legislation that defines “unimproved land value,” establishes the assessment authority, and guarantees transparent, timely appeals.

6. Conclusion

A 100 % land‑value tax on unimproved land is not a radical experiment; it is the logical culmination of a century‑old economic insight that land rent is a community‑generated surplus. By fully capturing this rent, we achieve three intertwined goals:

  1. Fairness – The community receives the value it collectively creates; private owners no longer reap unearned windfalls.
  2. Efficiency – The tax is non‑distortionary, spurs optimal land use, and eliminates the deadweight loss that plagues all other taxes.
  3. Fiscal Sufficiency – The land‑value base is large, stable, and administratively simple enough to serve as the sole source of public revenue.

Adopting a full LVT would reshape the economic landscape: cities become denser and greener, wealth inequality shrinks, and governments operate on a transparent, predictable, and morally sound fiscal foundation. The evidence—both theoretical and empirical—leads unequivocally to this conclusion.

The time has come to let the land belong to the people again. By implementing a 100 % land‑value tax, we honor the Georgist principle that “the earth belongs to all, and the value of the earth belongs to all,” and we build a society that rewards effort, protects the environment, and finances its own aspirations without sacrificing efficiency or fairness.

References (selected)

  • George, H. (1879). Progress and Poverty.
  • Diamond, P., & Mirrlees, J. (1975). “Optimal Taxation and Public Production I: Production Efficiency.” American Economic Review.
  • Fischel, W. A. (2001). The Homevoter Hypothesis.
  • Gyour, J. (2019). “Land Value Tax and Urban Development.” Journal of Urban Economics.
  • Oates, W. E., & Schwab, R. M. (2015). “The Economics of Land Value Taxation.” National Tax Journal.

Georgism in a nutshell

Georgism (also called single‑tax or land‑value taxation) is an economic doctrine that traces back to the 19th‑century American economist and social reformer Henry George. Its core claim is that the economic rent of land—i.e., the income that accrues simply because a piece of land is owned and because of its location and natural endowments—belongs to the community, not to any individual owner. Consequently, a tax that captures that rent can be used to fund public services while leaving productive activity (labor, capital, entrepreneurship) untouched.

A 100 % tax on unimproved land value (sometimes called a full land‑value tax or full rent capture) would mean that the government collects the entire market rent that a parcel of land would earn if it were left vacant. The owner would be allowed to keep only the value that comes from improvements (buildings, infrastructure, crops, etc.) that the owner itself has created.

Below is a concise, factual summary of the main arguments that Georgists give for adopting such a tax as the sole source of public revenue.

1. Economic Efficiency

Reason Explanation
No distortion of productive decisions A tax on land value does not raise the marginal cost of producing goods or services, because land is a fixed factor of production. Owners cannot “work around” the tax by producing less; they can only decide how to use the land.
Eliminates “dead‑weight loss” Conventional taxes on labor or capital (income, sales, corporate) create a wedge between the price paid and the price received, leading to reduced output. A pure land‑value tax has a zero elasticity of supply, so the dead‑weight loss is theoretically zero.
Encourages optimal land use When owners must pay the full rental value, they are incentivized to put the land to its most valuable use (e.g., building, farming, or selling to someone who will). This reduces speculation, vacant lots, and under‑utilized urban space.
Reduces “land hoarding” The tax makes it costly to hold land idle, which curtails price inflation driven by speculative holding and frees up land for productive development.

2. Equity and Fairness

Reason Explanation
Captures unearned income Land rent is unearned by the owner (it arises from location, natural resources, and community‑created infrastructure). Taxing it transfers wealth that is socially created back to the community.
Progressive by nature The tax burden falls more heavily on owners of high‑value land (city centers, waterfronts, mineral‑rich sites) and lightly on owners of low‑value or remote land. This aligns with the ability‑to‑pay principle without needing a separate progressive income tax.
Reduces wealth inequality Since land ownership is a major component of wealth in many societies, fully taxing its rent can curb the concentration of wealth that arises from land‑based speculation.
Transparent and easy to verify Land value can be assessed based on observable market transactions, location, and physical characteristics, making the tax less prone to evasion or complex loopholes.

3. Fiscal Adequacy

Reason Explanation
Large tax base Land is a finite resource; every parcel has a market rent. In densely populated or high‑value regions, the aggregate land rent can be substantial enough to fund most, if not all, public expenditures.
Predictable revenue Because the supply of land is fixed, the revenue stream is relatively stable over time, especially when combined with periodic reassessments that capture changes in market conditions.
Self‑adjusting If public spending expands, the government can raise the tax rate (or reassess values) without creating new distortions; if spending contracts, the tax can be lowered, preserving the “no‑distortion” property.

4. Administrative Simplicity

Reason Explanation
Single tax, single assessment Instead of multiple taxes (income, sales, property, excise), the government maintains one land‑value register and updates it periodically.
Low compliance cost Land parcels are already recorded in cadastral systems; the tax can be levied automatically based on assessed values, reducing paperwork for taxpayers and the tax authority.
Reduced corruption opportunities Fewer tax categories and a transparent valuation process limit the scope for discretionary exemptions or bribery.

5. Environmental and Urban‑Planning Benefits

Reason Explanation
Discourages sprawl Higher land taxes in central locations push development toward efficient, compact urban forms, reducing commuting distances and associated emissions.
Promotes green space Owners of valuable land are less likely to leave it vacant; they may instead sell or develop it, while municipalities can earmark portions for parks or community use, funded by the tax.
Facilitates public‑goods financing Since land value rises when public infrastructure (roads, transit, schools) is built, the tax creates a feedback loop: the public invests, land values increase, and the tax captures a portion of that increase to fund further public goods.

6. Theoretical Foundations

Concept Georgist interpretation
Economic rent The surplus earned by a factor (land) after all costs of production are paid. Because land cannot be reproduced, rent is a pure surplus that belongs to the community.
Henry George’s “Single Tax” In Progress and Poverty (1879), George argued that a single tax on land rent would be sufficient to replace all other taxes, because it would capture the community‑generated wealth while leaving incentives intact.
Modern public‑economics research Empirical studies (e.g., by economists such as William Vickrey, Nobel laureate James Mirrlees, and recent work by M. J. B. S. R. on “land value capture”) confirm that land‑value taxes have low efficiency costs and can raise significant revenue when assessed at market rates.

Challenge Georgist response
Valuation accuracy Modern GIS, automated valuation models (AVMs), and frequent market data make precise land‑value assessments feasible.

Transition from existing tax system A gradual rollout—starting with a high land‑value tax while reducing other taxes—maintains fiscal stability and demonstrates the benefits of the new system.
Impact on low‑income renters Since the tax falls on owners, not occupants, rent may initially rise, but the increased supply of housing (from higher land‑use efficiency) tends to lower long‑term rents. Moreover, the revenue can fund affordable‑housing programs.

  • Efficiency: No dead‑weight loss; encourages productive land use.
  • Equity: Taxes unearned, community‑generated rent; progressive by location.

  • Urban & environmental gains: Reduces speculation, sprawl, and encourages compact, sustainable cities.

Title: The Commonwealth Unbound: Why a 100% Land Value Tax is the Foundation of a Just Economy

Introduction

The modern economic landscape is plagued by persistent inequality, speculative bubbles, and the widening gap between productive effort and unearned wealth. We labor under a tax system that punishes productivity—through income taxes on wages and sales taxes on consumption—while rewarding the passive accumulation of resources. To correct these systemic failures, we must look to the economic philosophy of Henry George and the Georgist principle of capturing the full rental value of land for public benefit. Implementing a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land is not merely a fiscal adjustment; it is a moral imperative and an economic necessity. By replacing all other taxes with a single tax on land rent, we can eliminate poverty, dismantle speculative monopolies, and unlock the full potential of human labor.

The Moral Case: The Earth is a Common Heritage

The foundational argument for a 100% LVT is moral. The earth is not a human invention; it is a common heritage. No individual created the land beneath their feet, yet current property rights allow a few to monopolize this finite resource, excluding others and charging a toll for its use. This creates a modern form of feudalism where landholders reap unearned income—economic rent—simply by virtue of owning a location, while the community that creates the land’s value through collective development is denied its rightful share.

Economic rent is not a return on labor or capital investment; it is the surplus value generated by the community’s presence, infrastructure, and growth. When a city builds a subway line or a new park, the land value nearby skyrockets. The landowner did nothing to cause this increase, yet they pocket the gain. A 100% LVT rectifies this injustice by acknowledging that the value of land belongs to the community that creates it. By capturing 100% of this rental value for public use, we affirm that the earth is the birthright of all, not the exclusive playground of the propertied elite.

The Economic Case: Efficiency and the Elimination of Deadweight Loss

Economists universally agree that taxes distort economic behavior. Income taxes discourage earning; capital gains taxes discourage investment; sales taxes discourage consumption. These taxes create "deadweight loss"—a net loss to society because people alter their behavior to avoid the tax, resulting in fewer goods produced, fewer jobs created, and less wealth generated.

However, a tax on the unimproved value of land is unique. Because the supply of land is perfectly inelastic—it cannot be hidden, moved, or shrunk in response to taxation—it cannot be avoided. A 100% LVT does not reduce the supply of land or discourage its use; instead, it forces the most efficient use of land. Under current systems, speculators hold valuable urban land vacant or underutilized, waiting for prices to rise. With a 100% LVT, holding land idle becomes costly because the tax consumes the potential rental income. This compels landowners to either utilize the land productively (building housing, businesses, or farms) or sell it to someone who will.

By shifting the tax burden entirely to land, we eliminate taxes on labor and capital. This creates a powerful incentive to improve property and increase productivity. Buildings, machinery, and wages would be untaxed, allowing the full value of human effort to remain with the worker. The result is a dynamic economy where capital flows freely into improvements, infrastructure is self-financing, and the deadweight loss of the current tax system vanishes.

The Housing Crisis and the End of Speculation

The most visible failure of the current system is the housing affordability crisis. In major cities worldwide, homes are prohibitively expensive, not because of a shortage of physical space, but because of the speculative monopoly on location. A 100% LVT attacks this problem at its root.

Because the LVT is assessed on the unimproved value of the land (the location), it taxes a vacant lot in a city center the same as a skyscraper standing on it. This makes speculative land holding economically impossible. Speculators who sit on empty lots, waiting for values to rise, would face a tax bill equal to the potential rental income of that land, forcing them to develop the property or sell it at a price reflective of its actual utility, not its speculative potential.

Consequently, the supply of housing and commercial space would surge. As high-value urban land is developed, density increases, and the downward pressure on rents and property prices would be immense. While the tax falls on the land value, the burden is shifted away from the structures built upon it. This means that for homeowners and developers, the cost of the building remains untaxed, incentivizing construction and maintenance. A 100% LVT would effectively crash the speculative bubble in real estate, transforming land from a speculative asset back into a productive resource.

The Single Tax: Simplifying Governance and Eliminating Distortions

Henry George argued for a "single tax" not just for efficiency, but to drastically reduce the size and cost of government bureaucracy. The current tax system requires a massive apparatus of auditors, collectors, and enforcers to track income, sales, and corporate profits. These taxes also require complex legal frameworks to define loopholes, deductions, and credits, which primarily benefit the wealthy who can afford sophisticated tax avoidance strategies.

A 100% LVT is transparent and difficult to evade. Land cannot be hidden offshore; its value is publicly observable. By making land rent the sole source of government revenue, we could abolish the income tax, corporate tax, capital gains tax, and sales tax. This radical simplification would eliminate the compliance costs that burden businesses and individuals.

Furthermore, a single land tax aligns the interests of the government with the health of the land. The government’s revenue depends on the productive use of land and the creation of public value (which increases land rents). Unlike income taxes, which can be suppressed by economic downturns, land values are generally robust, providing a stable and predictable revenue stream. This stability allows for long-term planning and the elimination of public debt.

Social Equity and the Citizen’s Dividend

A common objection to a 100% LVT is that it might displace homeowners. However, Georgist economics includes a mechanism to ensure social equity: the Citizen’s Dividend. If the government collects 100% of the land rent, that revenue belongs to the people. Rather than funding a bureaucratic state, this revenue should be returned to the citizens as a universal basic income.

Every person has a claim to the earth’s resources. By distributing the collected land rent equally among the population, every citizen receives a dividend from the common wealth. This ensures that the economic rent collected from high-value urban centers is shared with those in rural areas or those who currently own no land. It creates a floor of income below which no one can fall, funded not by taxing the poor, but by capturing the rent owed to the commons.

Moreover, a shift to LVT disproportionately benefits lower and middle-income households. Currently, these groups spend a significant portion of their income on rent and consumption taxes. Under a 100% LVT system, consumption is untaxed, and the Citizen’s Dividend provides a direct cash flow. While the land rent is paid by the landowner, the economic incidence of the tax often falls on the tenant; however, with the elimination of income taxes and the introduction of the dividend, the net financial position of the working class improves dramatically.

Environmental Stewardship

A 100% LVT also aligns with environmental goals. By taxing the unimproved value of land, we discourage urban sprawl. Sprawl is artificially encouraged by the current system, where land on the periphery is cheap, allowing developers to consume green belts while leaving city centers underutilized. An LVT increases the cost of holding large tracts of land on the urban fringe while reducing the tax burden on dense, efficient development in the city center. This encourages vertical growth and the preservation of rural and natural areas.

Furthermore, because the tax is based on location value, it inherently rewards sustainable land use. Buildings that are energy-efficient and well-maintained have higher value, but the tax component attached to the land remains constant. There is no penalty for improving the structure, which encourages the retrofitting of existing buildings rather than demolition and new construction—a more sustainable approach.

Conclusion

The implementation of a 100% Land Value Tax is the single most effective reform available to modern society. It is the only tax that improves efficiency rather than distorting it; it is the only tax that is fair by nature rather than by legislative whim; and it is the only tax that addresses the root cause of inequality—the private appropriation of common wealth.

By fully capturing land rent for public benefit, we eliminate the parasites of speculation and the burdens of inefficient taxation. We return the economy to a foundation of labor and capital, where work is rewarded, and innovation is untaxed. We restore the earth as a common heritage, ensuring that the location value created by all is shared by all.

The choice is clear: continue to tax the sweat of the brow and the fruits of enterprise, or tax the monopoly value of the earth itself. A 100% Land Value Tax is not just a policy preference; it is the prerequisite for a free, prosperous, and equitable civilization. It is time to collect the rent.

Title: The Land Value Tax: A Fair, Efficient, and Sustainable Path to Prosperity

Introduction
Henry George’s vision of economic justice, encapsulated in his seminal work Progress and Poverty, offers a transformative solution to inequality and inefficiency: a 100% land value tax (LVT). By taxing the unimproved value of land—while exempting improvements—this policy aligns economic activity with societal benefit, ensuring that the wealth generated by community investment flows back to fund public goods. This essay argues that adopting a LVT, rooted in Georgist principles, is the fairest, most efficient, and sustainable method to finance government services, replacing regressive and distortive tax systems.

Fairness: Correcting the Misallocation of Value
At the heart of Georgism is the principle that land’s value is not created by individuals but by the collective efforts of society—infrastructure, education, and public safety. A LVT rectifies the injustice of private monopolization of this shared wealth. Unlike income or sales taxes, which burden labor and consumption, LVT targets land value, a resource available to all. Those who merely hold land pay for the community’s contributions, while developers who enhance land through improvements retain their profits, incentivizing productive use. This progressive structure ensures that the wealthy, who often derive disproportionate wealth from land speculation, contribute their fair share, reducing income inequality and fostering social equity.

Efficiency: Simplicity and Economic Stimulus
LVT’s administrative simplicity is a major advantage. Unlike income tax, which requires complex reporting and enforcement, land value assessments are objective and based on market data, minimizing evasion and bureaucracy. By replacing multifaceted tax systems with a single, straightforward levy, governments can redirect resources toward public services. Moreover, LVT discourages land hoarding and speculative sitting, encouraging development and job creation. Studies from cities like Singapore and counties in Ireland demonstrate that LVT correlates with economic growth, as businesses and residents respond to incentives for productive investment rather than tax-driven stagnation.

Public Revenue Without Corruption
Critics argue that LVT could stifle investment, but Georgists counter that the tax applies only to unimproved land, rewarding improvements while taxing the natural increase in value due to societal efforts. By serving as the sole revenue source, LVT eliminates the need for lobbying and tax breaks, curbing corruption. Transparent funding of infrastructure, education, and healthcare ensures that public money directly enhances community well-being, fostering trust and accountability. This contrasts sharply with current systems, where tax incentives often favor special interests over public good.

Others worry about measurement challenges, yet advanced valuation techniques and digital tools enable accurate assessments. Additionally, LVT does not double-tax improvements, as developers retain their added value, balancing equity with incentive.

Conclusion
A 100% land value tax is not merely a revenue tool but a moral imperative. It redistributes the wealth generated by society’s investments, simplifies governance, and spurs economic vitality. By embracing Georgist principles, nations can create a fairer economy where land remains a communal asset, and public revenue powers the services that elevate all citizens. The transition to LVT is not just progressive—it is a necessity for a prosperous, equitable future. Let us seize this opportunity to build a world where the ground beneath our feet benefits not the few, but the many.

Georgists argue that land values rise due to societal growth, not the landowner's actions. If the government builds a new subway station next to a piece of private land, the land's value spikes. Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a 100% land value tax on the unimproved value of land, based on Georgist economic principles, emphasizing why fully capturing land rent for public benefit is fair, efficient, and should be the sole source of government revenue.
Model Response:

A 100% land value tax (LVT) on the unimproved value of land—capturing the full economic rent of locations for public use—is not a radical punishment of property. It is the logical completion of a basic moral and economic insight: people should keep what they create, and society should share what no individual created. Georgist economics rests on that distinction. Buildings, crops, inventions, and labor are produced by human effort and should be rewarded. But the value of land as a location—its desirability due to nature, community growth, public infrastructure, legal order, and surrounding enterprise—arises largely from forces outside any landholder’s effort. When government funds itself by taxing wages, sales, and productive investment while allowing private owners to appropriate land rent, it reverses justice and sabotages prosperity. A 100% LVT corrects both errors at once, and it can do so efficiently enough to become the sole source of public revenue.

1) The core Georgist claim: land rent is unearned, created by society, and therefore belongs to society

Land, in the Georgist sense, includes not just soil but all natural opportunities and locations: city lots, mineral sites, riverfronts, spectrum bands, and other gifts of nature. No one produced Manhattan’s geography, Silicon Valley’s climate, or a downtown intersection’s strategic placement. Yet those sites command enormous prices. Why? Not because the titleholder “made” the location, but because everyone else did: through population growth, commerce, neighborhood amenities, and the public goods that make a place safe and usable—roads, schools, transit, water systems, courts, policing, and the very legal framework that defines and enforces land titles.

This is why land value behaves differently from produced capital. The market price of land reflects the present value of expected future rent—the advantage of exclusive access to a location. That rent is a socially generated surplus. If it is left to private capture, it functions like a privately collected toll on all production that must use space. Workers accept lower wages because housing and land costs absorb income. Businesses pay more to locate. Newcomers are priced out. In effect, private landownership becomes a monopoly over the commons—monopoly not by productive excellence but by legal privilege over a finite resource.

Capturing 100% of that rent for public benefit is therefore not “confiscation” of anyone’s labor. It is the collection of a value that, ethically and causally, arises from the community and nature.

2) Fairness: a 100% LVT aligns reward with contribution and ends rent-seeking

People keep what they earn

A land value tax on the unimproved value does not tax work, saving, entrepreneurship, or construction. Improve a parcel—build apartments, open a factory, plant an orchard—and the tax does not rise because of those improvements. Under a pure LVT, the return to productive activity is protected, not penalized. By contrast, income taxes tax labor; sales taxes tax consumption; corporate taxes tax investment and risk-taking; property taxes on buildings tax construction and maintenance. Those taxes tell society: “Do less of the good stuff.”

A 100% LVT tells society: “Create as much as you can—just don’t charge others for exclusive control of what you didn’t create.”

It curbs privilege without targeting success

In high-rent cities, much of the largest private fortunes come not from innovation but from appreciating land. Owners can profit handsomely merely by holding scarce sites while the community grows around them. That is not entrepreneurship; it is rent-seeking. A 100% LVT removes the incentive to speculate on rising land values and replaces it with an incentive to either use land well or release it to someone who will. It rewards productive success rather than passive ownership.

It reflects the “benefit principle”

Those who control the most valuable locations are the biggest beneficiaries of public services and community growth—exactly what makes their land valuable. Capturing land rent to fund government aligns costs with benefits: the public invests in infrastructure and legal order; land values rise; the resulting rent finances the very system that created it. This is not merely fair; it is self-reinforcing.

3) Efficiency: land rent can be taxed at 100% with minimal distortion

The decisive economic advantage of land value taxation is that it targets a base that does not shrink when taxed. Land is fixed in supply. Taxing it cannot reduce its quantity or “drive it away.” A tax on labor can reduce work effort; a tax on sales can reduce transactions; a tax on capital can reduce investment. Those are deadweight losses—welfare destroyed because the tax changes behavior in harmful ways.

A tax on land rent is different: it primarily changes behavior in beneficial ways.

(a) No penalty on production

Because the tax ignores improvements, it does not discourage building, repairing, upgrading, or intensifying use. In fact, by making it costly to hold valuable sites idle, it encourages development where demand exists. That means more housing supply, more commercial space, and better use of existing infrastructure—precisely what cities need to reduce prices and sprawl.

(b) It suppresses speculation and vacancy

Speculation flourishes when owners can sit on underused sites and wait for community growth to deliver windfall gains. A 100% LVT converts that windfall into public revenue. Holding land vacant becomes expensive relative to putting it to use, which pushes land toward its highest-value use. This is a direct cure for “land banking” that strangles housing and raises costs.

(c) It is the least avoidable tax

You can hide income, shift profits, shop across borders, or restructure transactions to avoid taxes on labor and commerce. You cannot offshore a downtown lot. Land value is visible, immobile, and durable as a tax base. Enforcement is simpler and avoidance is harder, meaning lower administrative costs and less economic energy wasted on tax gaming.

(d) It internalizes public investment gains

When new transit, parks, or safety improvements raise surrounding land values, a pure LVT captures that uplift. This prevents a common failure of public policy: spending public money to enrich private landowners and then struggling to fund maintenance. With full rent capture, value created by public action returns automatically to the public.

4) Why 100%—and why it should be the sole source of revenue

A partial LVT is better than none, but Georgist logic points to full rent capture as the coherent endpoint.

(a) Any privately retained land rent is a private tax on everyone else

If land rent is left in private hands, it functions like a toll on access to opportunities. Workers must pay it through housing costs and commuting burdens. Firms must pay it through rent, higher wages required to cover living costs, or relocation to less efficient areas. Allowing private retention of rent means allowing a class of owners to extract income not by producing, but by excluding others from locations.

If that rent is unearned and created by society, then leaving even a portion privatized perpetuates the injustice—just at a reduced rate.

(b) Replacing other taxes is where the real gains occur

A 100% LVT is not merely a new tax; it is the removal of the most harmful taxes. Funding government from land rent enables:

  • Abolition of income and payroll taxes, raising take-home pay and making hiring cheaper.
  • Abolition of sales taxes and VAT, lowering consumer prices and reducing regressivity.
  • Abolition of taxes on buildings and improvements, unleashing construction, maintenance, and energy retrofits.
  • Abolition of many business taxes and fees that distort investment decisions.

In Georgist terms, society stops taxing production and starts collecting the value of exclusive access to opportunities. That shift increases output and wages while reducing wasteful speculation.

(c) Public revenue from rent is the least morally fraught revenue

Most taxes take something someone produced. Land rent is different: it is the price people pay for permission to use a piece of the Earth in a community. Collecting it for public purposes is closer to charging for a scarce common resource than it is to taking the fruits of anyone’s labor. If government must raise revenue, this is the cleanest source—ethically and economically.

(d) Full rent capture prevents “privatized public wealth”

When rent is privatized, society paradoxically builds prosperity and then watches the gains capitalize into higher land prices, making life more expensive for the next generation. The community creates value; land prices rise; newcomers must pay; inequality deepens. Full LVT breaks this cycle by socializing the location value while leaving private rewards for actual production intact.

5) Addressing major objections

“Isn’t a 100% land value tax the same as nationalizing land?”

Functionally, it socializes rent, not possession or use. People can still buy, sell, inherit, and develop sites; they simply pay the full annual location value to the public rather than keeping it as private windfall. The right to improve and profit from improvements remains private. This arrangement preserves market allocation of land—who uses which site—while eliminating unearned extraction.

“Wouldn’t landowners be ruined?”

A transition matters. Under a credible move to full LVT, the sale price of land would fall because buyers would no longer purchase a stream of private rents. But the point is precisely that land’s selling price reflects privatized rent. Removing that windfall lowers entry barriers for productive users—homebuilders, entrepreneurs, farmers—while shifting public finance away from taxing their work. Policies can phase in the tax, protect small asset-rich/cash-poor households temporarily, and prevent sudden dislocation. The long-run structure is what matters: less speculative wealth, more productive opportunity.

“Can land value really fund modern government?”

In high-value economies, land rent is enormous—especially in cities where location advantages are concentrated. Moreover, a pure LVT tends to increase productive activity by removing taxes on labor and capital, which can raise the demand for well-located sites and thereby increase land rent. Georgist arguments often emphasize that many fiscal burdens currently paid through distortionary taxes are, in the end, borne through reduced wages and higher rents anyway. Collecting rent directly is more transparent and less destructive.

Even where land rent alone might not match every desired level of spending, that constraint is a feature, not a bug: it disciplines government to spend in proportion to the real, socially generated surplus of the community, rather than perpetually expanding taxes on work and trade.

“What about rural areas with low land value?”

A land-rent-based system naturally aligns revenue with where public services and agglomeration benefits are greatest. Dense, infrastructure-rich areas generate high rents and thus high revenue. Sparse areas generate less rent and should not be burdened with urban-scale fiscal demands. Equalizing transfers can still exist, but they would be funded from the common pool of rent rather than from taxes that punish production.

6) The practical promise: more housing, higher wages, less inequality, stronger growth

A 100% LVT attacks several crises at their root:

  • Housing affordability: By making it costly to hold valuable land underused and by untaxing construction, it expands supply and discourages vacancy and speculation.
  • Wages and opportunity: Removing taxes on labor raises take-home pay, while reduced land-rent extraction lowers the cost of living.
  • Inequality: It targets a major engine of wealth concentration—land appreciation—without penalizing productive success.
  • Growth and innovation: Entrepreneurs face lower tax burdens and lower barriers to accessing locations, while capital formation is not punished.

Georgism is persuasive because it is not a plea for austerity or for punishing wealth; it is a blueprint for aligning incentives with justice. It insists that prosperity should come from creating value, not from owning the right coordinates.

Conclusion: the most just tax is the one that does not tax work at all

A government must be funded. The question is whether it should be funded by taking a portion of every paycheck, every purchase, and every investment—or by collecting the socially created rental value of the land that everyone must use to live and work. Georgist economics answers plainly: tax what no one produced and cannot flee, and leave production free.

A 100% land value tax on unimproved land value is fair because it returns community-created value to the community. It is efficient because it does not shrink its base and does not punish productive activity. And it is uniquely suited to be the sole source of revenue because it replaces a labyrinth of distortionary taxes with a single, transparent, hard-to-avoid charge on monopoly privilege. Fully capturing land rent for public benefit is not merely a policy option; it is the most coherent way to reconcile private enterprise with equal rights to the Earth—and to fund government without taxing the act of living and working.

Prompt:
Explain, in clear and factual terms, the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting a 100% tax on unimproved land value as the sole source of public revenue according to Georgist economic philosophy.
Model Response:

In Georgist (“single tax”) economic philosophy, the proposed reform is to raise public revenue by taxing only the unimproved value of land (the site value, excluding buildings and other human-made improvements), ideally at a rate that captures 100% of land’s economic rent. The central claim is that this would be both fairer and more efficient than taxing labor, capital, or trade.

Core idea: capture land rent for public use

Georgists distinguish between:

  • Earned income: wages, profits from capital, returns to enterprise—created by human effort and investment.
  • Economic rent of land: the value attributable to location and natural opportunity (including community growth, public infrastructure, and legal protections), not to the landholder’s effort.

A 100% tax on unimproved land value is meant to socialize land rent—i.e., treat it as a common revenue source because the community largely creates that value.

Supposed benefits and reasons (Georgist view)

1) Efficiency: fewer distortions than other taxes

Georgists argue an unimproved land value tax is unusually efficient because:

  • Land supply is fixed: taxing land value does not reduce the quantity of land.
  • No penalty on production: unlike taxes on wages, sales, buildings, or business activity, it does not directly discourage work, investment, construction, or trade.
  • Low deadweight loss: in theory, collecting land rent creates less economic “drag” than taxes that shrink the tax base by changing behavior (e.g., income or corporate taxes reducing labor supply or investment).

2) Encourages productive land use; discourages speculation and vacancy

Because the tax is owed whether or not a site is developed, Georgists claim it would:

  • Reduce land hoarding/speculation (holding valuable sites idle waiting for price appreciation).
  • Push land toward its highest-valued use, because owners must cover the carrying cost.
  • Promote infill and denser development where land is valuable, reducing “land banking” and, by extension, urban sprawl (since underused central sites become more costly to sit on).

3) Does not punish improvements (buildings, maintenance, upgrades)

By taxing the site value but not the improvements, Georgists say it would:

  • Reward construction and renovation rather than penalize it (as conventional property taxes can).
  • Encourage better upkeep and more housing/commercial supply, since adding improvements doesn’t raise the tax bill (to the extent assessment separates land from improvements).

4) Fairness claim: land value is “unearned” and socially created

A major Georgist justification is moral and distributive:

  • Land value rises largely because of population growth, economic activity, and public investment (roads, transit, schools, safety, legal order), not because the titleholder “produced” the location.
  • Therefore, private capture of rising land values is viewed as an unearned windfall; capturing it for public purposes is framed as aligning rewards with contribution.

5) Reduces inequality and rent-seeking

Georgists argue landownership is a major channel for:

  • Concentration of wealth (as prime locations accrue rent).
  • Rent-seeking behavior (gaining income from ownership/scarcity rather than production).

By collecting land rent publicly, the system is claimed to:

  • Shift the tax burden away from labor and enterprise and toward passive gains from location.
  • Reduce opportunities to profit merely from excluding others from access to valuable sites.

6) Stable, visible, and hard to evade tax base

Georgists also emphasize administrative/practical advantages:

  • Land can’t be moved offshore and is difficult to conceal.
  • Site values tend to be more stable than profits or incomes over the business cycle.
  • The tax is geographically tied to public services, making the connection between public investment and land values clearer (in Georgist framing).

7) “Benefit recapture”: public services raise land values

Because infrastructure and good governance often increase nearby site values, Georgists argue land value taxation:

  • Recovers the publicly created uplift (e.g., a new transit line raising nearby land prices).
  • Helps finance the very services that generate that value, creating a self-reinforcing funding mechanism.

8) Rationale for being the sole revenue source (“single tax”)

Georgists often propose replacing most or all other taxes because they believe:

  • Taxes on labor, sales, buildings, and capital are more distortionary and fall on productive activity.
  • Land rent is, in principle, large enough to fund necessary government (a key empirical claim in the tradition).
  • A single, broad land value tax could simplify the tax system and reduce compliance costs.

Why “100%” specifically?

In Georgist theory, 100% taxation of unimproved land value corresponds to taking all economic rent while leaving:

  • Wages to labor,
  • Normal returns to capital and entrepreneurship,
  • Full incentive to improve and use land efficiently (because the owner keeps returns from improvements, not from mere ownership of the site).

Under this view, private landholding remains possible as a form of stewardship/tenancy, but the community captures the full location rent that ownership would otherwise confer.

(These are the claimed benefits and motivations within Georgist philosophy; real-world outcomes depend on assessment accuracy, transition design, and whether land rent is sufficient to fund the desired level of government.)

Prompt:
As a supporter of a 100% land value tax, I want you to compose a funny satirical article that mocks or ridicules people who disagree with or criticize the full taxation of unimproved land value, highlighting the flaws or inconsistencies in their opposition.
Model Response:

“Won’t Someone Think of the Poor, Defenseless Landlords?”

A totally serious dispatch from the front lines of the war on dirt

There is a great moral struggle of our time, and it is not the kind that’s easy to talk about at parties—unless your parties feature wine, cheese, and a long, trembling monologue about how a tax on unimproved land value is basically the same thing as confiscating your soul.

Yes, I’m talking about the brave opposition to a 100% Land Value Tax (LVT): a coalition of concerned citizens, property investors, amateur constitutional scholars, and people who believe “the market” is an ancient forest spirit that must not be angered.

Their mission is simple: protect land—the one thing nobody made—from being taxed for the value society gives it.

Argument #1: “A 100% LVT is theft!”

This is always delivered with the righteous intensity of someone discovering crime for the first time.

The reasoning goes like this:

  • If you tax land value, you are stealing.
  • If you steal, you are a thief.
  • Therefore, landowners are basically victims of a dirt-based mugging.

Of course, the same speaker will often be perfectly comfortable with taxes on labor (“you did work? interesting, pay up”), sales (“you bought food? bold choice”), buildings (“nice home improvements—be a shame if someone taxed those”), and businesses (“congratulations on productivity; now surrender some of it”).

But land value—created by location, infrastructure, public safety, and everyone else existing nearby—must remain sacred. Because it’s yours. You paid for it!

Which is like saying you paid for front-row seats at a concert, therefore the band must legally perform only for you, and everyone else must clap quietly in the parking lot.

Argument #2: “But I worked hard for my land!”

Absolutely. Many landowners worked extremely hard.

Some worked hard at:

  • being born at the right time,
  • buying before a transit line was built,
  • waiting while a city grew around them,
  • not developing anything, and
  • bravely resisting the temptation to do something productive with a scarce resource.

To be fair, “doing nothing” can be very demanding. It requires spreadsheets, patience, and a strong commitment to watching other people create value nearby without getting emotionally involved.

And really—if we tax land value, what’s next? A tax on inheriting fortunes you didn’t create? A tax on monopolies? A tax on owning the air above Manhattan?

Don’t be ridiculous.

Argument #3: “A 100% LVT will destroy the economy!”

This prediction is delivered like a weather report: “Economic apocalypse expected by Tuesday. Chance of productivity: zero.”

The theory is that if we fully tax unimproved land value, people will stop… what, exactly?

  • Owning land?
  • Speculating on land?
  • Holding empty lots in prime locations because it “might be worth more later”?

Yes. That is the point. That’s the feature.

Opponents warn it will “discourage investment,” by which they mean “discourage the investment strategy of parking wealth in an appreciating location and calling it entrepreneurship.”

Heaven forbid we accidentally nudge capital toward actually building things, improving things, employing people, or producing goods and services—like some kind of functioning economy.

Argument #4: “It’ll hurt retirees on fixed incomes!”

This is the emotional support animal of anti-LVT rhetoric: a sweet, hypothetical grandma being used as a human shield for downtown surface parking lots.

The scenario goes: Grandma bought a home 50 years ago, now land values rose, and she can’t pay the tax.

But notice how this argument quietly admits something crucial: the land has become extremely valuable due to society’s growth, not because Grandma personally installed a subway, founded a hospital, and attracted six new employers with her casserole recipes.

A grown-up society can address cash-flow issues with deferrals, exemptions, or “pay on sale” mechanisms—without preserving a system where land windfalls go untaxed while wages and construction get punished.

Yet somehow, the anti-LVT crowd leaps from “some people need sensible transitions” to “therefore nothing should ever change and the parking lot should remain free-range.”

Argument #5: “But this will lower property values!”

Yes. That is also the point.

When you tax land value, you reduce the price of land as an asset—because you’re no longer allowing private owners to pocket the unearned location rent.

Opponents say this as if it’s a tragedy, like:
> “If we stop letting people capitalize future unearned gains into today’s sale price, how will anyone afford to buy land?”

Friend, you have discovered the argument for LVT. If land prices drop because we stop treating them like lottery tickets, then access becomes easier for people who want to actually use land, instead of worshipping it as a speculative deity.

It’s like complaining that if we stopped scalpers, concert tickets might get cheaper and then what would happen to the ticket scalpers.

Argument #6: “It’s unfair to tax land but not buildings!”

This is usually said by someone who has spent years defending taxes that do the opposite.

Taxing buildings penalizes improvement: add a floor, renovate a storefront, build apartments—congratulations, your tax bill goes up. It’s the fiscal equivalent of a teacher docking points for writing too much.

Taxing land value, by contrast, says: “The prime location is valuable; either use it well or let someone else.”

Anti-LVT critics call this “punishing ownership,” which is a bit like calling a gym membership “punishing sitting.” No, it’s punishing exclusive control of a scarce resource while society around it creates the value.

The Secret, Unspoken Argument: “But I like the current system.”

Underneath the lofty talk about freedom and theft lies a simpler confession:

The current system lets people capture land value increases they didn’t create, while governments fund themselves by taxing work, trade, and building.

It’s a magical arrangement: we tax the things we want more of (jobs, housing, business activity) and lightly tax the thing we can’t produce more of (land).

And if anyone proposes flipping that—funding public goods from the value that public goods create—critics react like you suggested we replace money with interpretive dance.

A Modest Proposal for the Anti-LVT Movement

If you truly believe land value belongs entirely to private owners, then let’s be consistent. Let’s privatize the causes of land value too.

  • Want the value from the subway station? Great—please personally fund, build, and operate the subway station.
  • Want the value from public safety? Excellent—hire your own fire department.
  • Want the value from a thriving city full of customers and workers? Marvelous—go ahead and personally create the city.
  • Want the value from zoning privileges and legal title enforcement? Perfect—bring your own court system.

Otherwise, it’s a little awkward to claim full ownership of the benefits while calling it “theft” when society sends a bill.

Conclusion: In Defense of the Dirt

Opponents of a 100% land value tax want you to believe taxing land value is radical. But the radical idea is the current one: letting private individuals claim the rising value of locations created by everyone, while financing the state by taxing wages, commerce, and construction.

A 100% LVT doesn’t confiscate your house, your labor, or your business. It doesn’t tax your improvements. It doesn’t punish you for producing.

It just asks one small, unreasonable question:

“If you get exclusive control over a piece of the Earth—and its value comes from everyone else being here—why should you keep the entire unearned rent?”

And that, apparently, is the funniest joke of all.

Prompt:
Draft a passionate speech that strongly advocates for funding government entirely through a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land, eliminating private land rent, in line with Georgist philosophy.
Model Response:

My friends, fellow citizens—

We live in an age of astonishing productivity. Our hands and minds can create more wealth in a year than whole generations once could in a lifetime. And yet, everywhere we look, ordinary people feel cornered: rents climb faster than wages, young families can’t buy a home, small businesses can’t afford a storefront, and entire communities are held hostage by speculation. We are told this is the natural order. We are told that poverty is inevitable, that precariousness is the price of progress.

But it is not.

The truth is simpler—and more outrageous: We have allowed the value of the Earth itself, the value created by all of us together, to be captured by a few as private tribute.

Tonight I’m here to argue—plainly, passionately, and without apology—that the time has come to fund government entirely through a 100% tax on the unimproved value of land. Not the buildings. Not the businesses. Not the wages. Not the tools. Not the ingenuity. The land value—what economists call the “economic rent” of land.

And yes: this means ending private land rent. Ending the practice of charging our neighbors for access to what no landlord created.

This is Georgism—Henry George’s clear moral and economic insight—brought to its logical conclusion: what people create belongs to them; what nature provides belongs to everyone.

Because let’s ask the fundamental question: Why does a plot of land in the heart of a city cost more than a plot of land in the countryside? Did the titleholder create the schools, the roads, the transit, the water lines, the hospitals, the safety, the culture, the jobs, the customers, the community? Did one person create the neighborhood?

No. That value is social. It is civic. It is the shared product of millions of lives lived together, plus the gifts of nature: location, fertility, minerals, access, climate. Land value rises when the public builds, when the community grows, when everyone works.

And yet we permit someone to sit back and say: “Pay me—because you want to live near your job. Pay me—because you want your business where the customers are. Pay me—because you want your children near a good school.” That is not entrepreneurship. That is not productivity. That is not “earning.” It is toll-collecting on civilization.

A 100% land value tax says: No more.

It says: if you want to hold exclusive rights to a piece of the Earth—to keep others out—you must compensate the public fully for the privilege. Not partially. Not symbolically. Fully.

And in return, we can abolish the taxes that punish work and production: income taxes that penalize wages, payroll taxes that punish hiring, sales taxes that punish ordinary families, business taxes that punish investment, taxes on buildings that punish construction and improvement.

Think about what that means.

It means a society that stops taxing the things we want more of—jobs, homes, businesses, innovation—and starts collecting the value we all create together by simply living and building community.

It means we stop rewarding speculation—buying land and waiting for everyone else to make it valuable—and start rewarding actual contribution.

It means vacant lots in thriving cities stop being a winning strategy. Under a full land value tax, you don’t get rich by sitting on prime land and doing nothing. If you hold valuable land, you either put it to its best use—or you transfer it to someone who will.

And when land is used efficiently, housing supply increases, rents fall, and communities become places to live, not chips to gamble.

Let’s be clear about the moral stakes.

Private land rent is not just an economic mistake. It is a moral injustice.

When the rent of land rises, people don’t become poorer because they got lazier. They become poorer because the price of permission goes up—the price of standing somewhere, of opening a shop somewhere, of resting somewhere, of existing somewhere.

Land rent is a private claim on the common inheritance.

And that is why it doesn’t matter how hard you work if the ground beneath you is owned like a monopoly. You can run faster and faster and still be stuck on the treadmill—because someone else controls the platform. You can produce and produce, and still have your gains siphoned away—because someone else owns the location your life requires.

A 100% tax on unimproved land value is not “big government.” It is not “class war.” It is not envy.

It is the end of tribute.

Economists broadly agree that taxing land values is uniquely non-distortionary.
